questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of standard Binary Search on a sorted array of size n?
questions.explanation: Binary search cuts the search space in half at each iteration, yielding log2(n) comparisons in the worst case.

questions.question: Which of the following data structures operates on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle?
questions.explanation: A Queue processes elements in arrival order (FIFO), whereas a Stack is LIFO (Last-In, First-Out).

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of inserting an element at the end of a dynamic array (like std::vector or Python list)?
questions.explanation: Appending takes O(1) time normally; when the buffer doubles, copying takes O(n), averaging out to O(1) amortized.

questions.question: In a singly linked list with only a head pointer, accessing the k-th node takes O(1) time.
questions.explanation: False. Singly linked lists lack contiguous memory indexing; you must traverse sequentially from head in O(k) time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to retrieve the minimum element from a standard Min-Heap?
questions.explanation: The minimum element is stored directly at the root (index 0) of a Min-Heap, allowing O(1) peeking.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to build a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the bottom-up heapify algorithm?
questions.explanation: Bottom-up heap construction runs in mathematically proven O(n) linear time, not O(n log n).

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is guaranteed to be stable and have an O(n log n) worst-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: MergeSort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases (best, average, worst) and preserves the relative order of equal keys (stable).

questions.question: What algorithm is used to detect cycles in a singly linked list using two pointers (slow and fast)?
questions.explanation: Floyd's cycle detection advances a slow pointer 1 step and a fast pointer 2 steps; if they meet, a cycle exists.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (where height of single root is 1)?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree has 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(h-1) = 2^h - 1 nodes.

questions.question: Which tree traversal visits the root node first, followed by the left subtree, then the right subtree?
questions.explanation: Pre-order traversal visits Node -> Left -> Right.

questions.question: Performing an in-order traversal on a Binary Search Tree (BST) produces nodes in which order?
questions.explanation: Because in-order visits Left (smaller) -> Root -> Right (larger), it yields strictly non-decreasing sorted keys.

questions.question: In an AVL tree, what is the maximum allowed absolute difference between the heights of the left and right subtrees of any node?
questions.explanation: AVL trees enforce the balance factor condition: |height(left) - height(right)| <= 1 for every node.

questions.question: Which data structure is most commonly used to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS) in a graph?
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level using a Queue (FIFO), whereas DFS uses a Stack (or recursion).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's single-source shortest path algorithm using a Fibonacci or Binary Min-Heap?
questions.explanation: Using a standard binary min-heap, extracting min takes O(V log V) and edge relaxations take O(E log V), giving O((V + E) log V).

questions.question: Which algorithm can find the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph with possible negative edges (no negative cycles)?
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses dynamic programming to solve All-Pairs Shortest Path in O(V^3) time and handles negative edges.

questions.question: What is the primary condition for a directed graph to have a valid Topological Ordering?
options: It must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
It must be an Eulerian graph
questions.explanation: Topological sorting is only possible for DAGs; any cycle would create circular dependencies with no valid ordering.

questions.question: What collision resolution technique links all elements that hash to the same slot into a linked list or dynamic array?
questions.explanation: Separate chaining maintains a bucket list at each hash table index where collisions are appended.

questions.question: What is the optimal algorithm to find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray in an array of numbers?
questions.explanation: Kadane's algorithm computes the maximum contiguous subarray sum in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

questions.question: What data structure is ideal for implementing an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache with O(1) get and put operations?
questions.explanation: A Hash Map provides O(1) key-to-node lookups, while a Doubly Linked List allows O(1) removal and re-insertion at the head.

questions.question: With path compression and union by rank, what is the amortized time complexity per operation in a Disjoint Set Union (DSU)?
questions.explanation: The combination of union by rank and path compression achieves O(α(n)) practically O(1) since α(n) < 5 for all physical inputs.

questions.question: In the 0/1 Knapsack Problem with capacity W and n items, what is the standard dynamic programming time complexity?
questions.explanation: DP with items and weight states requires filling an n x W table, running in O(n * W) pseudo-polynomial time.

questions.question: What is the best possible time complexity to find the k-th smallest element in an unsorted array of n elements using QuickSelect?
questions.explanation: QuickSelect only recurses into one partition branch, achieving O(n) average time complexity.

questions.question: Which bitwise operation checks whether a positive integer n is a power of two?
questions.explanation: A power of two in binary has exactly one '1' bit (e.g., 8 is 1000). Subtracting 1 flips all lower bits (0111). Their AND is 0.

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity to find the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) in an array of n numbers?
questions.explanation: Using dynamic programming with patience sorting / binary search (std::lower_bound), LIS runs in O(n log n) time.

questions.question: What does the XOR operation evaluate to when applied to identical values: x ^ x?
questions.explanation: Any number XORed with itself produces 0 because identical bits cancel each other out.

questions.question: What specialized tree data structure is optimal for fast retrieval of keys by their prefixes (e.g., autocomplete)?
questions.explanation: A Trie stores common prefixes along paths from root, allowing word and prefix lookups proportional to word length O(L).

questions.question: What is the time complexity to update a point value and query a prefix sum in a Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)?
options: O(log n) update, O(log n) query
questions.explanation: A Fenwick Tree isolates lowest set bits (i & -i) to perform both point updates and prefix range queries in O(log n) time.

questions.question: Which Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) algorithm repeatedly adds the lowest-weight edge that connects a visited vertex to an unvisited vertex?
questions.explanation: Prim's algorithm grows a single tree cluster from a starting vertex, adding min-weight boundary edges via a priority queue.

questions.question: Which MST algorithm sorts all graph edges by weight and adds edges if they do not create a cycle using a Disjoint Set Union?
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges O(E log E) and greedily picks edges with DSU cycle detection.

questions.question: Which algorithm finds all Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) in a directed graph using a single Depth-First Search traversal?
questions.explanation: Tarjan's algorithm uses DFS discovery times and low-link values with a stack to identify all SCCs in O(V + E) single-pass time.

questions.question: What is the worst-case space complexity of a recursive Depth-First Search on a graph with V vertices?
questions.explanation: In a degenerate linear graph (a linked chain of nodes), the call stack depth reaches V frames, requiring O(V) space.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort when the pivot is always chosen as the minimum or maximum element?
questions.explanation: Extremal pivots split the array into sizes 0 and n - 1, producing an arithmetic progression of comparisons totaling O(n^2).

questions.question: Which algorithm can detect negative weight cycles in a directed graph?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times; if an edge can still be relaxed on the V-th pass, a negative cycle exists.

questions.question: How do you reverse a singly linked list in-place in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space?
options: Using an auxiliary stack of size n
questions.explanation: Three pointers (prev, curr, next) allow flipping node pointers iteratively without allocating extra memory.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in an unsorted array of size n?
questions.explanation: Without ordering or index mapping, linear search may need to examine all n items in the worst case.

questions.question: What data structure is optimal for solving the 'Next Greater Element' problem in O(n) time?
questions.explanation: A monotonic decreasing stack keeps indices of unresolved elements and resolves them as soon as a greater value appears.

questions.question: Which non-comparison sorting algorithm runs in O(n + k) time where k is the range of non-negative integers?
questions.explanation: Counting sort tallies frequency of each integer key in an auxiliary array of size k, running in O(n + k) time.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of standard MergeSort on an array of size n?
questions.explanation: Standard array MergeSort requires an auxiliary buffer of size n to merge halves, giving O(n) space complexity.

questions.question: What is the worst-case height of a Red-Black tree containing n nodes?
questions.explanation: Because the longest path (alternating red and black) is at most twice the shortest (all black), height is bounded by 2 * log2(n + 1).

questions.question: What is the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of nodes 4 and 6 in a BST where root is 5, left child is 3 (with children 2, 4), and right child is 7 (with children 6, 8)?
questions.explanation: In a BST, if one node is smaller than root (4 < 5) and the other is larger (6 > 5), the root (5) is their LCA.

questions.question: What preprocessing table does the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) pattern matching algorithm construct?
options: Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix (LPS array)
questions.explanation: KMP builds an LPS array in O(m) time to determine how far the pattern pointer can backtrack without re-checking matched characters.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of checking if a string of length n is a palindrome using two pointers?
questions.explanation: Starting one pointer at 0 and one at n-1 and moving inwards compares at most n/2 character pairs, running in O(n) time.

questions.question: Which algorithmic technique is most appropriate for finding the longest contiguous substring without repeating characters?
options: Sliding Window with a Hash Set
questions.explanation: A sliding window expands with the right pointer and contracts from the left when a duplicate character is encountered.

questions.question: What is the Dutch National Flag problem algorithm used to sort an array containing only 0s, 1s, and 2s in one pass?
options: Three-way partitioning with low, mid, and high pointers
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's three-way partitioning uses low, mid, and high pointers to partition the array in-place in O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.question: What algorithm finds the longest palindromic substring in an arbitrary string of length n in strictly linear O(n) time?
questions.explanation: Manacher's algorithm reuses previously computed palindrome radii to expand centers in guaranteed linear O(n) time.

questions.question: What rolling hash technique does the Rabin-Karp substring search algorithm use to achieve O(n + m) average time?
options: Polynomial rolling hash with modulo arithmetic
questions.explanation: Rabin-Karp computes a polynomial rolling hash that can be shifted right in O(1) time by subtracting the leading char and adding the trailing.

questions.question: How do you swap two variables a and b in-place without using a temporary third variable or arithmetic overflow?
options: a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b; a = a ^ b;
a = a & b; b = a | b; a = a ^ b;
questions.explanation: Three successive XOR operations swap the contents of two distinct memory locations without temporary storage.

questions.question: What is the recurrence relation for the Tower of Hanoi problem with n disks?
questions.explanation: Moving n disks requires moving n-1 disks to helper peg, 1 disk to target, and n-1 disks to target: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 = 2^n - 1.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of looking up a key in an ideal Hash Table with zero collisions?
questions.explanation: Computing the hash code and indexing directly into an array bucket executes in constant O(1) time.

questions.question: Which data structure allows efficient range minimum queries (RMQ) in O(1) time after O(n log n) preprocessing?
questions.explanation: A Sparse Table precomputes power-of-two intervals in O(n log n) time and answers idempotent queries like min/max in O(1) time.

questions.question: How can you determine if an undirected graph is bipartite?
options: Run 2-coloring via BFS/DFS; verify no two adjacent vertices share the same color
Calculate the determinant of the Laplacian matrix
questions.explanation: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles, which is verified by 2-coloring with BFS/DFS.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph with V vertices without self-loops or multi-edges?
questions.explanation: Every pair of distinct vertices can have at most one edge: C(V, 2) = V * (V - 1) / 2.

questions.question: Which algorithm finds the maximum flow in a flow network by augmenting along shortest paths using BFS in O(V * E^2) time?
questions.explanation: Edmonds-Karp implements Ford-Fulkerson using BFS for augmenting paths, proving polynomial upper bound O(V * E^2).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm for maximum cardinality bipartite matching?
questions.explanation: Hopcroft-Karp augments multiple shortest paths simultaneously per phase, achieving O(E * sqrt(V)) time complexity.

questions.question: Every tree with V vertices has exactly V - 1 edges.
questions.explanation: True. A fundamental definition of a tree is a connected acyclic graph, which always possesses exactly V - 1 edges.

questions.question: What graph structure represents dependencies between tasks where task A must precede task B?
questions.explanation: DAGs naturally model scheduling dependencies because directions indicate prerequisites and acyclicity prevents deadlocks.

questions.question: What is Kahn's algorithm used for in graph algorithms?
options: Topological Sorting using in-degrees and a queue
Finding bridges in an undirected graph
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly enqueues vertices with in-degree 0 and removes their outgoing edges to produce topological order.

questions.question: In an undirected connected graph, what is a bridge (cut-edge)?
options: An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components
An edge that belongs to all cycles
The edge with the highest weight in the graph
An edge connecting two leaf vertices
questions.explanation: A bridge is an edge whose deletion disconnects the graph into two separate components.

questions.question: What is an articulation point (cut-vertex) in a connected graph?
options: A vertex whose removal disconnects the graph
A vertex with in-degree equal to out-degree
The vertex with the highest degree
A root vertex of a spanning tree
questions.explanation: Removing an articulation point splits the remaining graph into two or more disconnected components.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of an Adjacency Matrix representation for a graph with V vertices?
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix allocates a 2D array of size V x V, consuming O(V^2) space regardless of the number of edges.

questions.question: In a 0-indexed binary heap array, what is the index of the left child of the node at index i?
questions.explanation: In 0-indexed complete binary trees, left child is 2i + 1, right child is 2i + 2, and parent is floor((i - 1) / 2).

questions.question: In a 0-indexed binary heap array, what is the index of the parent of the node at index i (i > 0)?
questions.explanation: Parent index is computed as floor((i - 1) / 2).

questions.question: What is the time complexity to build a Segment Tree over an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: A segment tree has 4n nodes and builds recursively bottom-up, performing constant work per node totaling O(n).

questions.question: What technique allows a Segment Tree to perform range updates (e.g., add val to range [L, R]) in O(log n) time?
questions.explanation: Lazy propagation postpones updates to child nodes until those subtrees are explicitly accessed, keeping range updates O(log n).

questions.question: What is the worst-case search time complexity in a standard Splay Tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: A single search in a splay tree can degrade to O(n) worst case, though any sequence of m operations has O(m log n) amortized time.

questions.question: Which self-balancing binary search tree maintains a random priority for each node satisfying both BST and Heap properties?
questions.explanation: A Treap maintains keys according to BST ordering and randomly assigned priorities according to Heap ordering.

questions.question: Which tree data structure is most widely used in relational database indexing (like MySQL InnoDB and PostgreSQL)?
questions.explanation: B+ trees have high fan-out (reducing disk I/O) and linked leaf nodes for ultra-fast sequential range scans.

questions.question: What is the diameter of a binary tree?
options: The number of nodes on the longest path between any two leaf/root nodes
The number of levels in the tree
The total count of all leaf nodes
The maximum degree of any node
questions.explanation: The diameter (or width) of a tree is the length of the longest path between any two arbitrary nodes in the tree.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to invert (mirror) a binary tree of n nodes?
questions.explanation: Mirroring visits every node once and swaps its left and right child pointers, running in O(n) linear time.

questions.question: What data structure can be used to evaluate an arithmetic expression written in Reverse Polish Notation (Postfix)?
questions.explanation: A Stack pushes operands and pops the top two operands whenever an operator is encountered.

questions.question: What is the state space size of the N-Queens problem on an N x N chessboard before pruning?
questions.explanation: Placing one queen per column naively yields N choices for each of N columns: N^N states (pruned to N! by row uniqueness).

questions.question: According to the Master Theorem, what is the asymptotic solution to the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)?
questions.explanation: Case 2 of Master Theorem applies: log_b(a) = log_2(2) = 1, f(n) = Theta(n^1), so T(n) = Theta(n log n) (MergeSort recurrence).

questions.question: What is the Master Theorem asymptotic solution to T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n^2)?
questions.explanation: log_2(8) = 3. Since f(n) = O(n^2) = O(n^(3 - epsilon)), Case 1 applies, yielding T(n) = Theta(n^3).

questions.question: What is the base case in computing factorial(n) recursively?
questions.explanation: 0! and 1! are mathematically defined as 1, which stops infinite recursive descent.

questions.question: What algorithm paradigm does the standard Binary Search belong to?
questions.explanation: Binary search divides the problem into halves, conquers the subproblem by choosing one half, and discards the other.

questions.question: What algorithm technique does Huffman Coding use to construct optimal prefix-free codes?
options: Greedy approach using a Min-Priority Queue
questions.explanation: Huffman coding greedily merges the two lowest frequency characters using a min-heap until a single tree remains.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to find the median of two sorted arrays of lengths m and n using binary search?
questions.explanation: By binary searching the partition cut on the smaller array, we find the median in optimal O(log(min(m, n))) time.

questions.question: How many subsets (power set) does a set of n distinct elements have?
questions.explanation: Every element has 2 choices (include or exclude), generating 2 * 2 * ... * 2 = 2^n subsets.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to generate all permutations of an array with n distinct elements?
questions.explanation: There are n! permutations, and creating/copying each permutation of length n takes O(n * n!) total work.

questions.question: What technique is used in Dynamic Programming to avoid recomputing overlapping subproblems when using top-down recursion?
questions.explanation: Memoization stores intermediate outputs in a lookup table (hash map or array) so each subproblem is solved only once.

questions.question: What does Brian Kernighan's algorithm count in O(number of set bits) time?
options: The number of 1s in the binary representation of an integer
The total digits of a number
The prime factors of a number
questions.explanation: In each loop n = n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, counting set bits in iterations equal only to the number of 1s.

questions.question: In an array where every element appears twice except for one single element, how can you find the single element in O(n) time and O(1) space?
options: Sum all elements and subtract min
questions.explanation: Because x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, duplicate pairs cancel out, leaving solely the unique element.

questions.question: What probabilistic data structure tests whether an element is definitely NOT in a set or MIGHT be in a set?
questions.explanation: Bloom filters use multiple hash functions over a bit array; false negatives are zero, but false positives are possible.

questions.question: What linked list data structure uses multi-level forward pointers with randomized heights to achieve O(log n) average search time?
questions.explanation: A Skip List builds layered express lanes via coin tosses, matching balanced tree search times with simpler linked logic.

questions.question: What is an XOR Linked List?
options: A memory-efficient doubly linked list storing pointer = address(prev) ^ address(next)
A linked list containing only boolean values
A list that supports O(1) arbitrary indexing
questions.explanation: An XOR linked list compresses two directional pointers into a single field by storing the XOR of prev and next node memory addresses.

questions.question: What is the result of shifting a positive integer x left by 1 bit (x << 1)?
questions.explanation: Each bit position corresponds to a power of 2; shifting left by k bits computes x * 2^k.

questions.question: What is the result of shifting a positive integer x right by 1 bit (x >> 1)?
questions.explanation: Shifting right by 1 drops the lowest bit, performing floor(x / 2).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Sieve of Eratosthenes to find all prime numbers up to N?
questions.explanation: The sum of reciprocals of primes converges to log(log N), giving O(N log(log N)) time.

questions.question: What is the Euclidean algorithm used for?
options: Computing the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of two integers
questions.explanation: Euclidean algorithm repeatedly applies gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until remainder is 0, running in O(log(min(a, b))).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Modular Exponentiation (a^b % m) using binary exponentiation?
questions.explanation: Repeated squaring divides the power b by 2 at each step, computing power in O(log b) multiplication operations.

questions.question: In JavaScript / Python, what does the two-sum problem ask and what is its optimal time complexity using a Hash Map?
options: Find two numbers adding up to target in O(n) time
Find two numbers adding to target in O(n^2) time
Find two numbers with max difference in O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Iterating through the array while checking if (target - num) exists in a hash map solves Two-Sum in O(n) time and O(n) space.

questions.explanation: Because fast travels at 2x speed, when fast reaches the end, slow has traveled exactly half the distance, landing on the middle node.

questions.question: What problem does the 'Trap Rain Water' classic problem solve, and what is the optimal two-pointer space complexity?
options: Calculates trapped water between elevation bars in O(n) time and O(1) space
Finds lake depth in O(n log n) time
Simulates hydraulic fluid in O(n^2) space
Computes rainfall probability in O(log n)
questions.explanation: Maintaining left_max and right_max pointers moving inward calculates trapped water column by column in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of edges in a tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: Any tree with n nodes has precisely n - 1 edges. Adding any edge introduces a cycle.

questions.question: Which of the following array operations takes O(n) time in a standard array of size n?
options: Reading an element by index arr[k]
Updating an existing element arr[k] = val
Popping the last element from fixed capacity array
questions.explanation: Inserting at index 0 requires shifting all n existing elements one position to the right, taking O(n) time.

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity to find the diameter of a binary tree in one traversal?
questions.explanation: A single post-order traversal computes each node's height while maintaining a global max of (left_height + right_height) in O(n) time.

questions.question: What data structure can maintain a sliding window maximum over an array of size n with window size k in O(n) total time?
questions.explanation: A monotonic deque maintains indices of elements in decreasing order of value, allowing O(1) amortized window maximum queries.

questions.question: How do you detect if a directed graph contains a cycle using DFS?
options: Check for back-edges pointing to a node currently in the active recursion call stack
Check if total edges > total vertices
Check if any node has in-degree > 1
questions.explanation: Three-state coloring (unvisited, visiting/in-stack, visited) identifies back-edges: visiting a node already in-stack proves a cycle.

questions.question: What is the Coin Change problem (minimum coins to make amount A) optimal time complexity using dynamic programming?
options: O(n * A) where n is number of coin denominations
questions.explanation: A 1D DP table of size A where dp[i] = min(dp[i - coin] + 1) iterates over n coins for each amount up to A, running in O(n * A) time.

questions.question: What algorithm determines whether a boolean formula in 2-Conjunctive Normal Form (2-SAT) is satisfiable in linear O(V + E) time?
options: Construct an Implication Graph and check if variable x and NOT x are in the same Strongly Connected Component (SCC)
questions.explanation: 2-SAT constructs an implication graph from clauses; formula is satisfiable if and only if no variable x shares an SCC with ~x.

questions.question: Which HTML5 semantic element represents the dominant, unique content of the <body> and should only appear once per page?
questions.explanation: The <main> element specifies the main content of the document, which must be unique and not repeated across pages (like headers/footers).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'alt' attribute on an tag in HTML?
options: Provides alternative text for screen readers and when the image fails to load
Specifies image alignment on the page
questions.explanation: The 'alt' attribute provides an alternative textual description for assistive technologies (screen readers) and fallback display.

questions.question: What does the ARIA attribute 'aria-live="polite"' instruct a screen reader to do?
options: Announce updates immediately, interrupting any ongoing speech
Wait until the user is idle before announcing dynamic DOM content changes
Mute all audio feedback on the page
Read content in a lower volume
questions.explanation: aria-live="polite" queues notifications to be spoken when the user finishes their current task, unlike "assertive" which interrupts.

questions.question: Which HTML input type renders a native mobile calendar picker on supported browsers?
questions.explanation: type="date" displays a native date picker dialog formatted to the user's operating system locale.

questions.question: What is the key difference between SVG and HTML5 Canvas?
options: SVG is XML-based vector graphics; Canvas is pixel-based raster bitmap
SVG is raster bitmap; Canvas is vector graphics
Canvas scales infinitely without blur; SVG pixelates
SVG cannot be styled with CSS
questions.explanation: SVG elements are vector nodes retained in the DOM (styleable with CSS), while Canvas draws raster pixels directly into a bitmap buffer.

questions.question: What feature of Web Components encapsulates internal styles and DOM markup from leaking into or being affected by page CSS?
questions.explanation: Shadow DOM provides scoped CSS and isolated DOM trees for web components so styles cannot accidentally conflict.

questions.question: Which meta tag ensures a web page scales properly across mobile viewports?
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag instructs mobile browsers to render the document at the device's physical pixel width rather than a zoomed-out 980px desktop view.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to embed client-side vector icons that can be styled dynamically with CSS fill and stroke?
questions.explanation: Inline <svg> tags become part of the DOM, allowing CSS rules like fill: currentColor and stroke-width to style them directly.

questions.question: What does the 'rel="noopener noreferrer"' attribute on external links (target="_blank") protect against?
options: Reverse tabnabbing where window.opener can redirect the originating tab to a phishing URL
questions.explanation: noopener ensures window.opener is null in the opened page, preventing malicious external sites from hijacking the parent tab.

questions.question: An HTML element can have multiple CSS class names separated by spaces in its 'class' attribute.
questions.explanation: True. class="btn btn-primary active" applies all three class rules to the element.

questions.question: In CSS Flexbox, which property aligns flex items along the cross axis (perpendicular to main axis)?
questions.explanation: justify-content aligns items along the main axis; align-items aligns items along the cross axis.

questions.question: What CSS rule centers a flex child both horizontally and vertically inside its container?
options: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;
display: flex; text-align: center; margin: auto 0;
display: block; margin: 0 auto; float: center;
questions.explanation: justify-content: center centers on main axis, and align-items: center centers on cross axis.

questions.question: Calculate the specificity score of this CSS selector: 'nav.main-nav ul li a:hover'
questions.explanation: ID count = 0; Classes/pseudo-classes count = 2 (.main-nav, :hover); Tag elements count = 3 (nav, ul, li, a -> actually 4 elements: (0, 2, 4)). Let's check: nav, ul, li, a are 4 elements. Closest standard specificity vector: 0 IDs, 2 classes/attributes, 4 elements.

questions.question: What CSS property specifies whether an element's padding and border are included in its total specified width and height?
questions.explanation: box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border within the declared width/height, preventing layouts from breaking.

questions.question: In CSS Grid, what expression creates responsive columns that wrap automatically without media queries, having minimum width of 250px?
questions.explanation: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) automatically creates as many 250px+ columns as can fit across the row.

questions.question: What new CSS feature introduced in modern browsers allows authoring style precedence layers without relying on selector specificity wars?
questions.explanation: @layer defines explicit priority orders for stylesheets (e.g. @layer reset, base, components, utilities), overriding selector specificity.

questions.question: What is the difference between CSS Container Queries (@container) and Media Queries (@media)?
options: Container queries query the size of a parent component container; Media queries query the browser viewport
Container queries query screen resolution; Media queries query parent width
Container queries only work in Flexbox; Media queries work in Grid
questions.explanation: @container allows a card or component to adapt its layout based on the exact width of its parent container rather than the global viewport.

questions.question: What CSS property defines custom variables in CSS?
questions.explanation: CSS custom properties are prefixed with double dashes: --primary-color: #3b82f6; and accessed via var(--primary-color).

questions.question: Why might a z-index of 9999 fail to display an element above another element with z-index of 1?
options: The element is trapped inside a different Stacking Context with a lower parent z-index
z-index maxes out at 1000 in CSS
questions.explanation: Stacking contexts (created by opacity < 1, transform, filter, will-change, or positioned elements with z-index) contain their children's z-indices.

questions.question: Which CSS pseudo-class matches an element only if it matches a selector passed as an argument (parent selector)?
questions.explanation: The :has() relational pseudo-class acts as a parent/previous sibling selector: e.g., card:has(img) styles a card containing an image.

questions.question: What will `console.log(typeof null)` output in standard JavaScript?
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, typeof null returns 'object'. This is a historical bug in the language's initial 32-bit type tag implementation that cannot be changed for backwards compatibility.
Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Next, the microtask queue empties (Promise .then prints 3). Finally, the macrotask/timer queue executes (setTimeout prints 2).

questions.question: What is a Closure in JavaScript?
options: A function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment
A method that closes an open network connection
A function that has no return statement
questions.explanation: A closure gives a function access to its outer scope variables even after the outer function has finished executing.

questions.question: How does the 'this' keyword behave inside an arrow function compared to a traditional function declaration?
options: Arrow functions do not bind their own 'this'; they inherit 'this' lexically from the enclosing scope
Arrow functions bind 'this' to the global window/global object strictly
Arrow functions can be rebound using .bind() or .call()
Arrow functions bind 'this' to the DOM element that fired the event
questions.explanation: Arrow functions lack their own 'this' binding and lexically resolve 'this' from the enclosing execution context.

questions.question: What does `Promise.allSettled(promises)` return compared to `Promise.all(promises)`?
options: Waits for all promises to settle (fulfill or reject) and returns an array of status objects without short-circuiting on rejection
Rejects immediately if any single promise rejects
Returns only the first promise that resolves
Cancels any ongoing promises after 5 seconds
questions.explanation: Promise.all rejects on the first failure, while Promise.allSettled waits for all promises to finish and returns their outcomes.

questions.question: What is the difference between '==' and '===' in JavaScript?
options: '==' performs type coercion before comparison; '===' checks both value and type without coercion
Both operators behave identically in ES6+
'==' is used only for comparing objects
questions.explanation: The strict equality operator (===) checks value and type without converting types; loose equality (==) coerces types (e.g. 0 == '0' is true, 0 === '0' is false).

questions.question: What does the Optional Chaining operator (?.) do in JavaScript?
options: Safely accesses nested object properties without throwing a TypeError if an intermediate reference is null or undefined
Creates a conditional ternary expression in one symbol
Checks if an array is non-empty
questions.explanation: user?.profile?.avatar short-circuits and evaluates to undefined rather than throwing 'Cannot read properties of undefined'.

questions.question: What is the Nullish Coalescing operator (??) in JavaScript?
options: A logical operator that returns its right-hand operand only when its left-hand operand is null or undefined
An operator that treats 0 and empty string '' as falsy and returns the right operand
questions.explanation: Unlike || which falls back on any falsy value (including 0, false, ''), ?? only falls back if the left operand is strictly null or undefined.

questions.question: What is a WeakMap in JavaScript, and how does it prevent memory leaks?
options: Keys must be objects, and keys are held weakly allowing them to be garbage collected if no other references exist
Keys can only be strings that expire after a timeout
Values cannot be overwritten once set
It is an array that automatically truncates its size
questions.explanation: In WeakMap, keys are weakly held object references. When an object key has no other references in memory, it is automatically garbage-collected.

questions.question: What JavaScript method creates a deep copy of a standard serializable object in modern browsers without external libraries?
questions.explanation: structuredClone() is a standard web API that recursively copies nested objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, and circular references.

questions.question: In DOM Event Propagation, what are the three sequential phases of an event?
options: Capturing Phase, Target Phase, Bubbling Phase
Target Phase, Bubbling Phase, Capturing Phase
Bubbling Phase, Processing Phase, Dispatch Phase
Initialization Phase, Execution Phase, Destruction Phase
questions.explanation: Events travel down from Window to target (Capturing), trigger on the target element (Target), and bubble back up to Window (Bubbling).

questions.question: What is Event Delegation in JavaScript DOM programming?
options: Attaching a single event listener to a common ancestor instead of separate listeners on dozens of child elements
Delegating event handling to a background Web Worker
questions.explanation: Event delegation leverages event bubbling to handle clicks on current and future child elements using event.target on a parent listener.

questions.question: What is the difference between `event.preventDefault()` and `event.stopPropagation()`?
options: preventDefault cancels the browser's default action (e.g. following a link); stopPropagation stops the event from bubbling up the DOM tree
stopPropagation cancels default actions; preventDefault stops bubbling
Both methods do the exact same thing
questions.explanation: preventDefault halts native browser behavior (submitting form, navigating anchor), while stopPropagation prevents parent handlers from catching the event.

questions.question: What browser API allows asynchronously monitoring when a DOM element enters or exits the viewport (e.g. for lazy-loading images)?
questions.explanation: IntersectionObserver efficiently detects when target elements intersect with an ancestor or top-level document viewport without scroll event lag.

questions.question: What browser storage mechanism persists data across browser tabs and sessions until explicitly cleared by user or code, with roughly 5-10MB capacity?
questions.explanation: localStorage persists across browser restarts and all tabs of the same origin. sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes.

questions.question: What cookie attribute prevents client-side JavaScript (`document.cookie`) from accessing the cookie, mitigating XSS token theft?
questions.explanation: The HttpOnly flag ensures that cookies can only be sent over HTTP requests and cannot be read via JavaScript document.cookie.

questions.question: What triggers a browser 'Reflow' (Layout calculation) versus a mere 'Repaint'?
options: Reflow recalculates geometry and positions of elements (e.g. offsetWidth, changing width/height); Repaint updates visual pixels (e.g. background-color)
Reflow only changes colors; Repaint changes element sizes
Both are identical operations in the browser engine
questions.explanation: Reflow is computationally expensive because changing geometry forces the browser to recalculate bounding boxes for the affected branch.

questions.question: What is a CORS preflight request, and which HTTP method does the browser issue for it?
options: An automated OPTIONS request sent before non-simple cross-origin requests to check server permissions
A GET request with custom headers
A HEAD request to check content length
questions.explanation: Browsers send an HTTP OPTIONS preflight request before complex requests (like PUT, DELETE, or custom headers) to verify Access-Control headers.

questions.question: What browser feature runs JavaScript scripts in background threads isolated from the main thread DOM?
questions.explanation: Web Workers execute heavy calculations in a separate background thread, communicating with the main thread via postMessage without freezing the UI.

questions.question: What technique delays function execution until a specified delay has elapsed since the last time the function was invoked (e.g., search input)?
questions.explanation: Debouncing groups rapid successive calls into a single invocation after quiet time, whereas throttling enforces a max execution rate.

questions.question: Why must React component state updates not mutate state directly (e.g., state.count = 5)?
options: React relies on object reference equality to detect changes and schedule component re-renders
Direct mutation crashes the V8 engine
State variables are frozen with Object.freeze automatically
Direct mutation only works in production builds
questions.explanation: React components re-render when state changes; mutating existing objects keeps the same memory address, bypassing shallow equality checks.

questions.question: What does the second argument (dependency array) in React's `useEffect(fn, deps)` control?
options: Specifies which state/prop values cause the effect function to re-run when changed
questions.explanation: An empty array [] runs the effect once on mount; specifying [a, b] runs the effect whenever a or b changes.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback` in React?
options: `useMemo` caches the calculated result of a function; `useCallback` caches the function definition itself
`useMemo` is for class components; `useCallback` is for function components
questions.explanation: useMemo(() => computeValue(a, b), [a, b]) returns a memoized value; useCallback(fn, deps) returns a memoized function reference.

questions.question: Why should you never use the array index as a 'key' prop for dynamic lists that can be reordered, sorted, or filtered in React?
options: Index keys confuse React's reconciliation diffing, causing component state or form input values to attach to the wrong elements
Index keys cause syntax errors in JSX
questions.explanation: When list items reorder or delete, their indices change, misleading React's diffing algorithm and causing subtle UI bugs.

questions.question: What does the `useRef` hook return in React?
options: A mutable object with a '.current' property that persists across renders without triggering a re-render when mutated
A read-only snapshot of component props
questions.explanation: useRef returns { current: initialValue }. Changing ref.current does not cause the component to re-render, making it ideal for DOM nodes and timer IDs.

questions.question: What was the primary goal of the React Fiber architecture rewrite?
options: To enable incremental rendering by splitting rendering work into chunks across animation frames and pausing/prioritizing updates
To eliminate the Virtual DOM entirely
To force static typing across all JSX components
questions.explanation: React Fiber turned the recursive stack reconciler into an incremental linked-list tree where work can be paused, aborted, or prioritized.

questions.question: What hook in React is designed to read layout from the DOM and synchronously re-render before the browser paints screen pixels?
questions.explanation: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after all DOM mutations but before the browser paints, preventing visual flickers when measuring DOM elements.

questions.question: What is a 'controlled component' in React form handling?
options: An input element whose value is driven by React state and updated via an onChange handler
A component that cannot be edited by the user
A component rendered on the server
An input using ref to read value on submit
questions.explanation: In a controlled component, form data is handled by a React component via value={state} and onChange={e => setState(e.target.value)}.

questions.question: What does React 18's `useTransition` hook allow developers to do?
options: Mark non-urgent UI state updates as transitions that can be interrupted by higher-priority urgent updates (like typing)
Transition between page routes in Next.js
questions.explanation: startTransition allows updates to be deprioritized so heavy renders don't block immediate user input like keypresses and clicks.

questions.question: What is the purpose of React Error Boundaries?
options: Catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app
Catch compile-time syntax errors in Babel
questions.explanation: Class components implementing componentDidCatch or static getDerivedStateFromError catch render-phase crashes and render fallback UI.

questions.question: What is the key difference between TypeScript `interface` and `type` alias?
options: Interfaces can be merged via declaration merging; type aliases cannot and can define unions/primitives
Type aliases cannot define object shapes
Interfaces compile to JavaScript functions; type aliases are deleted
There is no difference in TypeScript
questions.explanation: Multiple interface declarations with the same name merge their properties, while type aliases support unions (type X = A | B) and mapped types.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what does the utility type `Partial<T>` do?
options: Constructs a type with all properties of T set to optional (?)
Extracts only primitive properties from T
questions.explanation: Partial<T> wraps every property of type T in optional: { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] }.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what does the utility type `Record<K, T>` construct?
options: An object type whose property keys are K and property values are T
questions.explanation: Record<string, number> defines an object whose keys are strings and values are numbers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'unknown' type in TypeScript versus 'any'?
options: 'unknown' is type-safe; you must perform type checking or casting before performing operations on an unknown variable
'unknown' can only accept null or undefined
'unknown' is converted to number at runtime
questions.explanation: 'any' turns off type checking completely, whereas 'unknown' forces the developer to narrow the type via typeof, instanceof, or type guards.

questions.question: What TypeScript keyword is used to extract the return type of a function type inside a conditional type?
questions.explanation: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : any; uses 'infer' to deduce the return type variable R.

questions.question: What does the 'defer' attribute on an external `<script src="app.js" defer></script>` tag do?
options: Downloads the script in parallel and executes it only after HTML parsing is completely finished
Executes the script immediately, blocking HTML parsing
Delays downloading until the user scrolls
Loads the script inside an iframe
questions.explanation: defer scripts download in the background without blocking the parser and execute in document order right before DOMContentLoaded.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'async' and 'defer' attributes on script tags?
options: 'async' executes as soon as it downloads, potentially out of order; 'defer' executes after HTML parsing in document order
'defer' executes immediately; 'async' waits for document complete
'async' only works for CSS; 'defer' is for JS
questions.explanation: async scripts execute the moment they finish downloading, interrupting parsing; defer scripts execute orderly after DOM parsing completes.

questions.question: What Core Web Vital metric measures visual stability and unexpected layout shifts on a page?
questions.explanation: CLS measures unexpected shifts in visual elements as content loads, aiming for a score under 0.1 for good user experience.

questions.question: What Core Web Vital replaced First Input Delay (FID) to assess page responsiveness to user interactions?
questions.explanation: INP observes the latency of all click, tap, and keyboard interactions throughout the entire page lifecycle.

questions.question: Which HTTP header instructs the browser to enforce HTTPS connections exclusively for a domain?
questions.explanation: HSTS tells browsers to convert all insecure http:// requests to https:// automatically before network transmission.

questions.question: What security header helps prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks by restricting resource loading domains?
questions.explanation: CSP restricts which scripts, styles, images, and endpoints can be executed or loaded by the browser.

questions.question: In CSS, what does the unit 'rem' stand for?
questions.explanation: 1rem equals the font-size of the root <html> element (typically 16px by default).

questions.question: What is the difference between 'rem' and 'em' units in CSS?
options: 'rem' is relative to the root <html> font-size; 'em' is relative to the immediate parent element's font-size
'em' is relative to root; 'rem' is relative to parent
'rem' only applies to margins; 'em' applies to padding
They are identical in modern CSS
questions.explanation: em compounds based on the cascade of parent font-sizes, whereas rem remains consistently anchored to the root element.

questions.question: What CSS property creates a frosted-glass blur effect on content behind an element?
questions.explanation: backdrop-filter applies graphic effects (like blur or saturate) to the area behind an element with semi-transparent background.

questions.question: In JavaScript, what does `Object.freeze(obj)` do?
options: Prevents adding new properties, removing existing properties, or modifying values of existing properties (shallow)
Clones the object into an immutable Proxy
Deeply freezes all nested objects automatically
questions.explanation: Object.freeze makes an object shallowly immutable; properties cannot be added, removed, or changed.

questions.question: What is the difference between Array.prototype.map() and Array.prototype.forEach()?
options: map() returns a new array with transformed elements; forEach() executes a side effect and returns undefined
forEach() returns a new array; map() returns undefined
questions.explanation: map creates and returns a new array with the return value of each callback call; forEach returns undefined.

questions.question: What does Array.prototype.reduce() do in JavaScript?
options: Executes a reducer callback on each array element to accumulate them into a single resultant value
Shrinks the array length by half
questions.explanation: reduce runs an accumulator function across all elements, producing a single combined result (sum, object map, etc.).

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from a JavaScript array `arr` in a single line using ES6?
questions.explanation: Sets only store unique values, so [...new Set(arr)] or Array.from(new Set(arr)) discards duplicates.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Symbol' primitive data type introduced in ES6?
options: Creates completely unique, immutable identifiers often used as non-enumerable object property keys
questions.explanation: Every Symbol() call produces a unique value that cannot clash with other keys, even if initialized with identical descriptions.

questions.question: What JavaScript metaprogramming object allows intercepting and customizing operations like property lookups, assignments, and function calls?
questions.explanation: new Proxy(target, handler) intercepts fundamental operations (traps like get, set, has, deleteProperty) to customize behavior.

questions.question: What HTTP response status code signifies '204 No Content'?
options: The request succeeded, but the server has no response body to return
The server failed to locate the resource
questions.explanation: 204 indicates successful request completion without returning a message body (often used in DELETE or PUT operations).

questions.question: What is tree-shaking in modern JavaScript bundlers (Vite, Rollup, Webpack)?
options: Dead code elimination that analyzes ES module imports/exports to discard unused code from the production bundle
questions.explanation: Tree-shaking statically analyzes ES import/export graphs to strip out exported functions that are never imported or called.

questions.question: What is the CSS pseudo-class for styling an element when it receives keyboard focus, avoiding outline styling on mouse clicks?
questions.explanation: :focus-visible only applies focus indicators when navigation is initiated via keyboard (e.g. Tab key) rather than pointer clicks.

questions.question: What does CSS `pointer-events: none` do to an element?
options: Makes the element non-targetable for click, hover, and drag events, passing events through to underlying elements
questions.explanation: pointer-events: none causes mouse and pointer events to ignore the element and trigger on whatever is visually beneath it.

questions.question: What is the difference between `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` in CSS?
options: `display: none` removes the element from the document layout flow; `visibility: hidden` hides it while preserving its physical layout space
`visibility: hidden` removes it from layout flow; `display: none` preserves space
Both free the layout space equally
Only `display: none` hides text from screen readers
questions.explanation: display: none collapses the element so it occupies 0px in layout. visibility: hidden keeps the element's box in the DOM layout intact.

questions.question: What is the 'SameSite' cookie attribute option that prevents the cookie from being sent in all cross-site requests, including top-level navigations?
questions.explanation: SameSite=Strict withholds cookies on all cross-origin requests, including when clicking a normal hyperlink from an external domain.

questions.question: What lifecycle event fires when the HTML document has been completely parsed and DOM tree built, without waiting for stylesheets or images?
questions.explanation: DOMContentLoaded fires as soon as HTML is parsed into the DOM. The window 'load' event waits for all external resources (images, styles).

questions.question: What method stops an active `setInterval` timer in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: clearInterval takes the ID returned by setInterval and stops further scheduled recurring invocations.

questions.question: What CSS property optimizes performance by informing the browser ahead of time which properties on an element are expected to change?
questions.explanation: will-change: transform, opacity allows the browser to promote the element to its own GPU compositor layer before animation begins.

questions.question: Which of the following is a pure function in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: A pure function always returns the exact same output for the same arguments and produces zero observable side effects.

questions.question: What is JSX in React development?
options: A syntax extension for JavaScript that resembles HTML and compiles to React.createElement function calls
A separate programming language compiled to WebAssembly
A database query syntax for GraphQL
A JSON format for CSS styles
questions.explanation: JSX provides HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript, which compilers like Babel or SWC transform into React.createElement / jsx runtime calls.

questions.question: In React, what is 'prop drilling'?
options: The process of passing props through multiple levels of intermediate components that do not need the data themselves
questions.explanation: Prop drilling occurs when state must be passed down a deep component hierarchy, solved by React Context or state management stores.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the React Context API?
options: Provides a way to share values between components without having to explicitly pass a prop through every level of the tree
questions.explanation: React Context allows sharing global-like state (themes, authentication, locale) across an entire subtree.

questions.question: What happens when you call a state updater function in React with a callback: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`?
options: React passes the most recent guaranteed state value into the callback, avoiding stale closure race conditions in async operations
It runs the state update in a web worker
It executes synchronously before the next line of code
It resets the state to 0 first
questions.explanation: Functional state updates guarantee access to the current pending state rather than capturing stale values from old render closures.

questions.question: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) in modern web frameworks like Next.js or Nuxt?
options: Generating full HTML markup for a page on the server per request, sending rendered HTML to the client for faster initial paint and SEO
Executing JavaScript exclusively on user's GPU
Compiling client code into a single desktop binary
questions.explanation: SSR renders the component tree into HTML on the server, speeding up FCP/LCP and making pages immediately indexable by web crawlers.

questions.question: What is 'Hydration' in modern SSR frameworks?
options: Attaching event listeners and client React state to server-rendered static HTML markup to make it interactive
Cleaning memory leaks in the browser
Pre-fetching all images on the page
questions.explanation: Hydration bridges the gap between static HTML generated by the server and dynamic client-side React event handlers.

questions.question: What is the Fetch API return type in JavaScript?
options: A Promise that resolves to a Response object
questions.explanation: fetch(url) returns a Promise resolving to a Response object representing the HTTP response, which requires .json() or .text() to parse.

questions.question: Why does `fetch()` NOT reject its promise on HTTP 404 or 500 status codes?
options: A Promise from fetch() only rejects on network failures or CORS errors; HTTP 4xx/5xx are considered successful HTTP communications with response.ok = false
Because 404 is an informational status code
It is a bug in the Fetch spec that cannot be fixed
Because only POST requests can reject
questions.explanation: fetch only rejects if the network fails or request is blocked. 404 and 500 still represent completed HTTP exchanges, check response.ok.

questions.question: How can you abort an in-flight `fetch()` request in JavaScript?
options: Using an AbortController instance and passing its signal to the fetch options: { signal: controller.signal }
questions.explanation: const controller = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }); controller.abort(); cleanly cancels ongoing HTTP requests.

questions.question: What is the CSS clamp() function used for?
options: Clamping a value between an allowable minimum, preferred, and maximum value: clamp(min, preferred, max)
Fixing an element to screen viewport
questions.explanation: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem) creates fluid typography and dimensions that dynamically adapt to viewport size within strict bounds.

questions.question: What CSS property prevents text from wrapping onto a new line?
questions.explanation: white-space: nowrap prevents text sequences from breaking onto multiple lines.

questions.question: How do you truncate overflow text with an ellipsis (...) in CSS?
options: overflow: hidden; white-space: nowrap; text-overflow: ellipsis;
questions.explanation: The combination of overflow: hidden, white-space: nowrap, and text-overflow: ellipsis renders standard three-dot overflow truncation.

questions.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined` in JavaScript?
options: `undefined` means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value; `null` represents an intentional assignment of an empty value
`null` is a type of number; `undefined` is an object
They are identical in every context
questions.explanation: undefined indicates absence of value by default in uninitialized variables or missing parameters; null indicates explicit absence set by program logic.

questions.question: What does the JavaScript spread operator `...` do when applied to an array `[1, 2, ...arr]`?
options: Expands the iterable array elements into individual elements
Converts the array to a JSON string
questions.explanation: Spread syntax expands iterable items (arrays, strings, sets) in place into expressions or function argument lists.

questions.question: What is a 'polyfill' in web development?
options: A piece of code used to provide modern web functionality on older browsers that do not natively support it
questions.explanation: Polyfills emulate newer APIs (e.g. Promise, fetch, Array.prototype.flat) on legacy browser engines using backward-compatible code.

questions.question: Which CSS property specifies how image or video content should resize to fit its container box?
questions.explanation: object-fit: cover scales the media to maintain aspect ratio while filling the element box, clipping overflow.

questions.question: What does the CSS property `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;` achieve?
options: Maintains a 16:9 proportional ratio between element width and height automatically without padding hacks
Sets width to 16px and height to 9px
questions.explanation: aspect-ratio allows setting explicit proportions, preventing layout shift while responsive images load.

questions.question: In Web Performance, what is 'Code Splitting'?
options: Splitting application JavaScript bundles into smaller chunks that can be loaded dynamically on demand using dynamic import()
Dividing frontend and backend code into separate Git repositories
Running code across multiple CPU threads
questions.explanation: Code splitting ensures users only download the code needed for their current route or interaction, dramatically cutting initial bundle payload.

questions.question: What is the difference between client-side routing (Single Page Application) and traditional multi-page navigation?
options: Client-side routing intercepts anchor clicks and updates the view via JavaScript History API without reloading the entire page
Client-side routing requires reloading HTML on every link click
Client-side routing cannot update the browser URL bar
Client-side routing only works over WebSockets
questions.explanation: SPAs use history.pushState() to update the URL and render new component views client-side without full-page server round-trips.

questions.question: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA) Service Worker lifecycle event that allows caching app shell assets offline?
options: 'install' event (caches static assets using the CacheStorage API)
questions.explanation: During the Service Worker 'install' event, event.waitUntil() caches essential HTML, CSS, and JS files into CacheStorage for offline resilience.

questions.question: What does the 'A' stand for in the database ACID acronym?
questions.explanation: Atomicity guarantees that all operations within a transaction either succeed completely or are completely rolled back (all-or-nothing).

questions.question: Which SQL JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matched rows from the right table, filling unmatched right columns with NULL?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves all rows from the left table regardless of whether a matching record exists in the right table.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clauses in SQL?
options: WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation; HAVING filters aggregated groups created by GROUP BY
HAVING filters rows before aggregation; WHERE filters groups
WHERE can only be used with primary keys; HAVING with foreign keys
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows prior to grouping and aggregation; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY evaluation (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).

questions.question: What is a 'Clustered Index' in relational database systems (like MySQL InnoDB)?
options: An index that defines the physical storage order of table rows on disk (usually the Primary Key)
An index stored in a secondary text file
An index that only applies to foreign keys
questions.explanation: A clustered index dictates the actual on-disk arrangement of data rows; a table can therefore have only one clustered index.

questions.question: What is a 'Covering Index' in database query optimization?
options: An index that contains all columns requested by a SELECT query, allowing the database to serve results without reading table row data (index-only scan)
An index that covers all tables in a schema
An index that automatically encrypts table data
A composite index with more than 10 columns
questions.explanation: When an index contains every column needed by the query, the engine satisfies the request directly from the B-tree leaf nodes without table lookups.

questions.question: In database transaction isolation levels, what is a 'Phantom Read'?
options: A transaction re-reads a range of rows and discovers new rows inserted or committed by another concurrent transaction
A transaction reads uncommitted data that is later rolled back
A transaction modifies a row that was deleted
A database server crash during recovery
questions.explanation: Phantom reads occur when a query using a WHERE range predicate returns different sets of rows on repeated execution due to concurrent inserts.

questions.question: Which transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may still allow Phantom Reads under standard ANSI SQL?
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read guarantees that any row read during the transaction maintains its values on subsequent reads, but phantom rows may appear unless serializable.

questions.question: What does the SQL command `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` do in PostgreSQL or MySQL?
options: Executes the query, displays the chosen query execution plan, and reports actual runtime costs and row counts per node
Analyzes the database schema for syntax errors
Backs up the query results to S3
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the SQL statement, revealing sequential scans, index scans, hash joins, and real execution times to help optimize queries.

questions.question: What normal form requires that a table is in 1NF and all non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (no partial dependencies)?
questions.explanation: 2NF eliminates partial dependencies where a column depends on only part of a composite primary key.

questions.question: What normal form requires that a table is in 2NF and contains no transitive dependencies (non-key columns depending on other non-key columns)?
questions.explanation: 3NF requires that every non-prime attribute depends on 'the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key'.

questions.question: Which SQL constraint ensures that all values in a column are distinct and not duplicate?
questions.explanation: The UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate values in a column, automatically creating a unique B-tree index.

questions.question: What is the difference between `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE` in SQL?
options: `DELETE` removes rows one by one and can be rolled back; `TRUNCATE` deallocates data pages as DDL, resetting auto-increment counters and running much faster
`TRUNCATE` can use a WHERE clause; `DELETE` cannot
`DELETE` drops the table schema; `TRUNCATE` does not
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is a fast DDL command that deallocates storage pages directly without logging individual row deletions.

questions.question: In SQL window functions, what does `DENSE_RANK()` do compared to `RANK()` when there are tied values?
options: `DENSE_RANK()` does not skip rank numbers after ties (1, 1, 2); `RANK()` leaves gaps (1, 1, 3)
`RANK()` does not skip rank numbers; `DENSE_RANK()` leaves gaps
questions.explanation: RANK skips ranks after ties (e.g. 1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK assigns consecutive numbers without gaps (e.g. 1, 1, 2).

questions.question: What is an SQL injection vulnerability and how is it primarily prevented?
options: Attackers inject malicious SQL into input fields; prevented by using Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements)
A virus infecting the database server; prevented by antivirus software
Hardware failure in SSD storage; prevented by RAID
Exceeding database connection limits; prevented by connection pooling
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries separate SQL code structure from user input data, ensuring inputs are treated strictly as literal values, never executable code.

questions.question: What is a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) in database engines like PostgreSQL and SQLite?
options: A log where all data changes are written to persistent disk before applying them to database data files, ensuring durability and crash recovery
A log of failed user login attempts
A cache for SQL query results
A backup mechanism that runs once a week
questions.explanation: WAL ensures durability: in case of sudden power loss, uncommitted buffer pool pages can be reconstructed by replaying the sequential WAL log.

questions.question: What type of NoSQL database is MongoDB?
questions.explanation: MongoDB stores records as flexible, schema-less BSON (Binary JSON) documents organized into collections.

questions.question: What is Redis primarily known for?
options: An ultra-fast in-memory key-value data structure store used for caching, session management, and pub/sub
A relational database for complex joins
A file system for video streaming
questions.explanation: Redis stores data in RAM with optional persistence, providing sub-millisecond responses for strings, hashes, lists, sets, and sorted sets.

questions.question: What is the 'Cache-Aside' (Lazy Loading) caching pattern?
options: Application checks the cache first; if cache miss, reads from database, writes to cache, and returns data
Database automatically updates the cache on every commit
Application writes only to cache; background thread writes to DB
All reads bypass the cache completely
questions.explanation: In Cache-Aside, the application code manages cache reading and population on demand only when a cache miss occurs.

questions.question: What is the 'Cache Stampede' (Thundering Herd) problem?
options: When a popular cached key expires, and hundreds of concurrent requests simultaneously hit the database to recompute it
When the cache server runs out of disk space
When an attacker floods the cache with random keys
questions.explanation: A cache stampede overwhelms the database when high-traffic keys expire; mitigated using mutex locks, probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), or background refresh.

questions.question: What is the difference between Cache Penetration and Cache Breakdown?
options: Penetration queries non-existent keys that bypass cache and hit DB repeatedly; Breakdown occurs when a hot cached key expires under high load
Penetration is a hardware failure; Breakdown is software error
Both terms mean the exact same thing
questions.explanation: Cache Penetration queries keys that don't exist in DB (fixed via Bloom filters or caching nulls); Cache Breakdown is a single hot key expiring.

questions.question: What Redis data structure maintains elements ordered by a floating-point score, ideal for real-time gaming leaderboards?
questions.explanation: Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET) use a skip list and hash table to support O(log N) insertion, rank lookups, and range queries by score.

questions.question: What probabilistic Redis data structure estimates the unique cardinality of billions of items using only 12KB of memory?
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates unique counts (like daily active visitors) with a standard error of ~0.81% using negligible fixed memory.

questions.question: What is the CAP Theorem trade-off during a network partition in a distributed data store?
options: You must choose between Consistency (all nodes see latest data) or Availability (every non-failing node returns a response)
You must choose between Performance and Encryption
You must choose between Relational schemas and JSON
You must choose between RAM and Disk storage
questions.explanation: When network communication between nodes is severed (Partition), a system can either refuse requests to preserve consistency (CP) or accept writes risking inconsistency (AP).

questions.question: What does Eventual Consistency mean in distributed databases (like Apache Cassandra)?
options: If no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually converge to become identical over time
Transactions are consistent only on weekends
The database guarantees strict sequential execution
Writes fail if a single node is offline
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency trades off immediate synchronization for high availability and low latency, guaranteeing convergence over time.

questions.question: What is Database Sharding?
options: Horizontally partitioning a database table rows across multiple independent physical server instances
Creating read-only replicas in the same data center
Converting tables from SQL to NoSQL
questions.explanation: Sharding splits large datasets across multiple machines (by user_id, hash, or geographic region) to scale write throughput and storage.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is defined by RFC 7231 as idempotent and used to replace an entire resource representation?
questions.explanation: PUT is idempotent: calling PUT with the same payload multiple times results in the exact same resource state as calling it once.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is specifically designed for partial modifications to an existing resource?
questions.explanation: PATCH applies partial delta updates to a resource (e.g. updating just an email field) rather than replacing the complete object.

questions.question: What HTTP status code should a backend API return when a client request lacks valid authentication credentials?
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized indicates that the request lacks valid authentication credentials (e.g. missing or expired Bearer token).

questions.question: What HTTP status code should be returned when the user is authenticated, but lacks permissions to access the requested resource?
questions.explanation: 403 Forbidden means the server recognizes the caller's identity, but the caller lacks authorization/role privileges for that action.

questions.question: What HTTP status code indicates that the server encountered a rate-limiting threshold violation?
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests informs the client they have sent too many requests in a given amount of time (often paired with Retry-After header).

questions.question: What common performance issue in GraphQL occurs when resolving nested relational fields without batching?
questions.explanation: Fetching 10 authors and then issuing 1 query per author to fetch their books yields 1 + 10 = 11 database queries, solved by DataLoader batching.

questions.question: What underlying transport protocol does gRPC use to enable multiplexing, binary serialization, and bidirectional streaming?
questions.explanation: gRPC runs over HTTP/2, leveraging binary header compression, single TCP connection multiplexing, and Protocol Buffers serialization.

questions.question: What is the key difference between WebSockets and Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
options: WebSockets provide full-duplex bidirectional communication; SSE provides unidirectional server-to-client streaming over standard HTTP
SSE is bidirectional; WebSockets is unidirectional
WebSockets only work on mobile devices
questions.explanation: WebSockets allow both client and server to send messages freely; SSE streams text events strictly from server to client over persistent HTTP.

questions.question: What are the three dot-separated components of a JSON Web Token (JWT)?
questions.explanation: A JWT consists of base64url-encoded Header (algorithm/type), Payload (claims/user data), and cryptographic Signature (HMAC/RSA).

questions.question: Why should sensitive secrets (like passwords or credit card numbers) never be stored inside a JWT payload?
options: The payload is only base64url encoded, NOT encrypted; anyone with the token can decode and view its JSON content
Because JWT payloads max out at 64 characters
questions.explanation: JWT signatures ensure authenticity and tamper-proofing, but the payload itself is plaintext readable by simply decoding base64url.

questions.question: Which cryptographic password hashing algorithm incorporates an adjustable work factor (cost) to defend against hardware brute-force attacks?
questions.explanation: bcrypt and Argon2 use deliberate computational slowness and unique salts to make GPU and ASIC brute-force password cracking impractical.

questions.question: What is a 'Salt' in password storage?
options: A unique random string appended to each password before hashing to prevent rainbow table attacks
An encryption key shared among all users
A backup copy of the password
questions.explanation: Salting ensures identical passwords produce distinct hashes, rendering precomputed lookup tables (rainbow tables) completely useless.

questions.question: In OAuth 2.0 for single-page and mobile apps, what security extension replaces client secrets to prevent authorization code interception?
questions.explanation: PKCE generates a dynamic code_verifier and code_challenge pair, preventing attackers from intercepting and redeeming the authorization code.

questions.question: What rate-limiting algorithm uses a bucket that holds tokens arriving at a constant rate, allowing short bursts while enforcing an average rate?
questions.explanation: Token Bucket allows bursts up to bucket capacity and refills at a steady rate, balancing elasticity with steady-state rate control.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of a Message Broker like Apache Kafka or RabbitMQ?
