questions.question: What major efficiency improvement was introduced in the TLS 1.3 handshake compared to TLS 1.2?
options: Reduced the handshake from 2 round-trips (2-RTT) down to 1 round-trip (1-RTT) and deprecated weak legacy ciphers (RSA key exchange, CBC, RC4)
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 cuts connection latency in half (1-RTT) and supports 0-RTT resumption while stripping away obsolete and insecure cipher suites.

questions.question: What is an HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)?
options: A cryptographic construction that combines a secret key with a cryptographic hash function (SHA-256) to verify both data integrity and authenticity
A hardware MAC address on a motherboard
An encryption algorithm for hard drives
questions.explanation: HMAC ensures that a message has not been altered in transit and was originated by a party possessing the shared secret key.

questions.question: What default port is used for standard unencrypted HTTP traffic versus encrypted HTTPS traffic?
options: Port 80 for HTTP; Port 443 for HTTPS
Port 443 for HTTP; Port 80 for HTTPS
Port 22 for HTTP; Port 21 for HTTPS
Port 8080 for HTTP; Port 8443 for HTTPS
questions.explanation: HTTP defaults to TCP port 80; HTTPS defaults to TCP port 443.

questions.question: What default port is used for SSH (Secure Shell) remote server administration?
questions.explanation: SSH operates on TCP port 22 by default.

questions.question: What is a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack?
options: An attacker secretly intercepts and relays communications between two parties who believe they are directly communicating with each other
Flooding a router with fake emails
questions.explanation: MitM attacks intercept unencrypted traffic (or exploit fake certificates) to eavesdrop or tamper with communication data in real time.

questions.question: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
options: A vulnerability where malicious client-side JavaScript is injected into trusted web applications and executed in victims' browsers
questions.explanation: XSS allows attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in victims' browsers, hijacking session cookies, redirecting users, or defacing sites.

questions.question: What is the difference between Stored XSS and Reflected XSS?
options: Stored XSS permanently saves the malicious payload in a database; Reflected XSS reflects the payload off the immediate web server via URL parameters
Reflected XSS is stored in the database; Stored XSS is in URLs
Stored XSS only affects mobile phones
There is no difference in attack impact
questions.explanation: Stored XSS (persistent) affects everyone who visits a compromised page; Reflected XSS requires tricking a victim into clicking a crafted URL link.

questions.question: What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?
options: An attack that tricks an authenticated user into executing unwanted actions (e.g. money transfer or email change) on a trusted web application
Stealing passwords via fake login pages
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic inclusion of session cookies with cross-site requests, executing state-changing actions without user consent.

questions.question: How do Anti-CSRF Synchronizer Tokens defend against CSRF attacks?
options: A secret, unpredictable cryptographic token is embedded in user forms; requests are rejected if incoming requests lack the matching token
They encrypt all HTML tags with AES
They log out the user after 30 seconds
questions.explanation: Because an external attacker cannot read or forge the unique per-session anti-CSRF token, forged cross-site form submissions fail server validation.

questions.question: What is a SYN Flood attack in Denial of Service (DoS)?
options: Flooding a target server with bogus TCP SYN packets without responding to SYN-ACKs, exhausting the server's half-open connection backlog table
Flooding an email inbox with spam
questions.explanation: SYN floods exhaust connection state memory; mitigated using 'SYN Cookies' which encode state inside the initial sequence number without allocating RAM.

questions.question: What is Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)?
options: An attack where a vulnerable web server is coerced into sending unauthorized HTTP requests to internal, inaccessible backend services or cloud metadata APIs
questions.explanation: SSRF tricks backend servers into querying internal IPs (like AWS metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254) to leak secrets or access private subnets.

questions.question: What is a 'Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use' (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability?
options: A security flaw where a resource's status or permission changes in the brief window between when the software checks it and when it uses it
questions.explanation: In TOCTOU, an attacker swaps a validated file with a symbolic link to /etc/shadow right before the program writes to it, escalating privileges.

questions.question: What security principle states that every program and user should operate using the minimum privileges necessary to complete their job?
questions.explanation: Least Privilege minimizes damage: running web servers as non-root users ensures compromised services cannot alter system files directly.

questions.question: What is 'Defense in Depth' in cybersecurity?
options: Employing multiple layered defense mechanisms (firewalls, WAF, encryption, IAM, auditing) so that if one fails, others stop the attack
Hiding source code in secret folders
questions.explanation: Defense in Depth ensures no single security flaw compromises the entire system; multiple protective layers must be breached.

questions.question: What is a Web Application Firewall (WAF) such as AWS WAF or Cloudflare WAF?
options: A Layer 7 security proxy that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic to block common web attacks like SQLi, XSS, and malicious bot scraping
A hardware router on consumer desks
A virus scanner for desktop computers
questions.explanation: A WAF filters application layer traffic against OWASP Top 10 rule sets before requests reach the origin web application.

questions.question: What is Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)?
options: A memory-protection defense that randomizes the memory locations of program stack, heap, and libraries, making buffer overflow exploits unreliable
A tool for sorting array items
questions.explanation: ASLR prevents attackers from reliably jumping to known hardcoded function addresses (e.g. system() in libc) in memory.

questions.question: What is a 'Zero-Day' vulnerability?
options: A security vulnerability that is actively exploited in the wild before the software vendor has developed or released a security patch
A bug discovered on day 0 of a company's founding
A software trial that expires immediately
questions.explanation: Zero-day means developers have had zero days to fix the flaw; no official patch is yet available to protect users.

questions.question: What is Phishing in social engineering?
options: Deceptive emails, messages, or websites masquerading as legitimate entities to trick victims into revealing credentials or sensitive data
Stealing copper cables from telephone poles
questions.explanation: Phishing preys on human psychology rather than software bugs, convincing users to enter passwords into fake login portals.

questions.question: What is Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)?
options: Requiring two or more distinct verification factors (something you know, something you have, something you are) to gain account access
Using passwords with at least 20 characters
Logging in from two computers simultaneously
questions.explanation: MFA combines knowledge (password), possession (authenticator app/hardware token), or inherence (fingerprint) to thwart credential stuffing.

questions.question: What is Ransomware?
options: Malware that covertly encrypts a victim's files and demands payment (usually cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key
An antivirus scanner that costs money
questions.explanation: Ransomware locks critical enterprise files with strong encryption, threatening permanent data destruction if ransom demands are not met.

questions.question: What does the `chmod 755 filename` command do in Linux?
options: Owner has Read, Write, Execute (7); Group and Others have Read and Execute (5)
Everyone has full access to the file
Only root can access the file
questions.explanation: 7 = 4(r) + 2(w) + 1(x). 5 = 4(r) + 1(x). 755 is the standard permission mode for executable scripts and directories.

questions.question: What does `chmod 600 id_rsa` do to an SSH private key file?
options: Sets Read and Write permissions for the owner only; removes all permissions for Group and Others (enforced by OpenSSH)
Makes the key public on the internet
Shares the key with all users in the group
Locks the key from being read by anyone
questions.explanation: OpenSSH rejects private keys with permissive permissions, requiring chmod 600 (owner read/write only) to prevent unauthorized access.

questions.question: What is an Air-Gapped computer system?
options: A computer system that is physically isolated from the internet and any other unsecure local networks to guarantee ultimate security
A laptop cooled by high-powered air fans
A cloud server running in an airplane
questions.explanation: Air-gapping prevents remote network intrusions by physically severing all network interfaces and cables from critical infrastructure.

questions.question: What is DNS Poisoning (DNS Spoofing)?
options: Corrupting a DNS resolver cache with fraudulent IP addresses to redirect legitimate users to malicious attacker-controlled servers
Crashing a DNS server with heavy traffic
Sending infected emails to network admins
questions.explanation: DNS cache poisoning injects fake records into recursive resolvers, tricking browsers into navigating to phishing duplicates of bank portals.

questions.question: What security extension adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records to protect against DNS cache poisoning?
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs DNS responses with cryptographic key chains, allowing resolvers to verify the authenticity of IP address answers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Linux `/etc/passwd` file?
options: Stores basic user account information (username, UID, GID, home directory, shell)
Stores encrypted user passwords in plaintext
questions.explanation: Historically it contained passwords; today encrypted password hashes are stored safely in the restricted `/etc/shadow` file.

questions.question: Which Linux signal cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored by any process, immediately terminating it?
questions.explanation: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are handled directly by the kernel and cannot be intercepted, making `kill -9` the ultimate unconditional process terminator.

questions.question: What is the difference between `SIGTERM` and `SIGKILL` in Unix/Linux?
options: `SIGTERM` asks the process to gracefully terminate and clean up resources; `SIGKILL` forcibly kills the process immediately via kernel
`SIGKILL` can be handled by a catch block; `SIGTERM` cannot
questions.explanation: Standard practice is sending SIGTERM first to allow graceful shutdown (closing database pools, flushing logs), escalating to SIGKILL if unresponsive.

questions.question: What is a Stateful Firewall compared to a Stateless Packet Filtering Firewall?
options: A stateful firewall tracks active connection states (TCP handshakes, UDP streams) and automatically allows legitimate return traffic
A stateless firewall stores logs in MySQL
A stateful firewall is made of physical hardware only
questions.explanation: Stateful inspection understands connection context: once an outbound connection is permitted, incoming packets matching that active flow are permitted.

questions.question: What is a Botnet?
options: A network of compromised private computers or IoT devices infected with malware and controlled centrally by a threat actor (botmaster)
A group of AI chatbots talking to each other
A server cluster for training neural networks
questions.explanation: Botnets (like Mirai) are weaponized to launch coordinated multi-terabit Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks worldwide.

questions.question: What is a Smurf Attack in networking?
options: A DDoS attack where ICMP broadcast echo requests are sent with the spoofed source IP of the victim, causing hundreds of network devices to flood the victim
Cracking Wi-Fi passwords with blue lasers
A Trojan horse disguised as a video game
questions.explanation: The Smurf attack is an amplification attack that exploits IP broadcast addresses to overwhelm a victim's network with ICMP replies.

questions.question: What is Honeypot in network defense?
options: A decoy system intentionally deployed to lure, detect, and analyze attacks from malicious threat actors without risking production assets
A trap to catch software pirates
questions.explanation: Honeypots mimic production systems to alert security teams to intrusion attempts and study attackers' tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

questions.question: What is Keylogger malware?
options: Malware that covertly records every keystroke pressed by a user on their physical or virtual keyboard to harvest credentials and credit card numbers
Software that logs SSH key fingerprints
A tool for generating cryptographic keys
questions.explanation: Keyloggers capture sensitive typed text (passwords, emails, bank numbers) and exfiltrate the logs to a remote command-and-control server.

questions.question: What does the `sudo` command stand for and do in Unix/Linux?
options: 'Superuser Do': permits authorized users to execute commands with the security privileges of the superuser (root) or another user
questions.explanation: sudo allows granular privilege elevation logged in `/var/log/auth.log`, avoiding the security risks of sharing the raw root account password.

questions.question: What is the standard loopback IP address representing the local machine in IPv4?
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 (and the entire 127.0.0.0/8 block) routes packets locally within the host operating system loopback interface without hitting network hardware.

questions.question: What does binding a server socket to IP `0.0.0.0` mean compared to `127.0.0.1`?
options: `0.0.0.0` listens on all available network interfaces (LAN, Wi-Fi, Ethernet); `127.0.0.1` listens only for internal connections from localhost
`127.0.0.1` exposes the server to the public internet
questions.explanation: Listening on 127.0.0.1 is safe for local development; 0.0.0.0 exposes the port to the entire local network and internet.

questions.question: What is Port Scanning in network reconnaissance?
options: Probing a target host's network ports (using tools like Nmap) to discover open services, running daemon versions, and potential vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: Nmap sends packets (e.g. SYN scan) to ports 1-65535, identifying which application services (HTTP, SSH, MySQL) are actively listening.

questions.question: What is an Air-Drop or Watering Hole attack in cybersecurity?
options: Compromising a specific legitimate website frequently visited by a target organization to infect visitors with targeted malware
Flooding an office with fake emails
questions.explanation: Watering hole attacks infect high-profile niche industry websites where target employees congregate, waiting for victims to browse the site.

questions.question: What is a Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) exploit?
options: An advanced exploit technique that chains together existing small machine instruction sequences ending in 'ret' ('gadgets') to bypass non-executable stack protections (W^X / DEP)
A method for returning functions in Python
questions.explanation: When Data Execution Prevention (DEP) stops direct shellcode execution on the stack, ROP hijacks the stack pointer to chain existing executable library instructions.

questions.question: What is a Rootkit?
options: A stealthy type of malicious software designed to hide its presence and unauthorized administrator access deep inside the operating system kernel
questions.explanation: Rootkits hook low-level kernel system call tables to hide their own processes, files, and network sockets from system diagnostic tools like `ps` and `netstat`.

questions.question: What is a VPN (Virtual Private Network) and which modern protocol is celebrated for its lightweight 4,000-line codebase and high speed?
questions.explanation: WireGuard provides encrypted site-to-site or client-to-gateway tunnels using modern cryptography (ChaCha20, Curve25519) with exceptional speed and minimal attack surface.

questions.question: What command in Linux searches for exact string patterns inside files or directories?
questions.explanation: grep (Global Regular Expression Print) searches text files using literal strings or regular expressions.

questions.question: What command in Linux displays current disk space usage across all mounted file systems in human-readable format?
questions.explanation: `df -h` (Disk Free - Human readable) shows percentage used, available gigabytes, and mount points across all storage partitions.

questions.question: What does the command `kill -9 1234` do in Linux?
options: Sends an uncatchable SIGKILL to immediately terminate the process with PID 1234
Lowers the CPU priority of process 1234 by 9
questions.explanation: kill -9 sends signal 9 (SIGKILL) directly through the kernel, forcing immediate unconditional process destruction.

questions.question: What is the Linux `/proc` filesystem?
options: A pseudo-filesystem in RAM created dynamically by the kernel that exposes kernel parameters, hardware status, and running process info
A folder where user documents are stored
A backup directory on the hard drive
A file system for external USB drives
questions.explanation: /proc files occupy 0 bytes on disk; reading /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo, or /proc/[pid]/status retrieves live kernel data structures.

questions.question: What is an SSH Key Pair and why is it safer than password authentication?
options: Uses 4096-bit RSA or Ed25519 asymmetric cryptography; private keys never leave the client machine, defeating brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks
SSH keys can only be typed on special keyboards
questions.explanation: SSH key authentication uses challenge-response cryptography: the server verifies ownership of the private key without the key ever traversing the network.

questions.question: What does `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` do?
options: Generates a modern, high-speed, compact Elliptic Curve cryptography key pair for SSH authentication
questions.explanation: Ed25519 provides superior security, resistance to side-channel attacks, and ultra-short key lengths compared to traditional RSA.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `ssh-agent` utility?
options: A background daemon that holds decrypted private keys in memory so users don't have to re-enter passphrases on every SSH connection
An AI assistant for the terminal
A program that hacks remote servers
questions.explanation: ssh-agent keeps private keys in RAM; `ssh-add` loads keys once per session, securely answering authentication challenges.

questions.question: What is an Ingress Controller in Kubernetes network security?
options: A reverse proxy (like Nginx or Envoy) that manages external HTTP/HTTPS routing, SSL termination, and load balancing into Kubernetes service clusters
A firewall that blocks outgoing traffic
A storage device inside container pods
questions.explanation: Ingress controllers translate external requests into internal cluster IPs, enforcing TLS certificates and hostname-based routing.

questions.question: What is BPF / eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) in the modern Linux kernel?
options: A revolutionary kernel technology that allows executing sandboxed bytecode inside the Linux kernel dynamically without modifying kernel source or loading modules
questions.explanation: eBPF enables ultra-high-performance network packet filtering, observability (Cilium), tracing (bpftrace), and security enforcement directly inside the kernel.

questions.question: What is a 'Clickjacking' attack and how does the `X-Frame-Options` HTTP header prevent it?
options: Tricking a user into clicking transparent iframe elements layered over benign buttons; prevented by setting `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or frame-ancestors in CSP)
questions.explanation: X-Frame-Options: DENY forbids other domains from embedding the web page inside an <iframe>, neutralizing invisible overlay clickjacking.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Vulnerability Assessment and a Penetration Test (Pen Test)?
options: Vulnerability assessment automatedly identifies known vulnerabilities; Penetration testing actively attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to achieve objectives
Vulnerability assessments take down production servers
questions.explanation: Vulnerability scanning catalogs weaknesses with tools; pen testing simulates real-world adversaries chaining exploits to breach systems.

questions.question: What is a Red Team vs Blue Team exercise in enterprise cybersecurity?
options: Red Team acts as offensive adversaries attempting to breach defenses; Blue Team actively detects, defends, and responds to the attacks
Red Team writes code; Blue Team tests code
Red Team builds servers; Blue Team installs cables
They are video game tournament teams
questions.explanation: Red Teams challenge organizational readiness by simulating realistic cyber attacks, while Blue Teams harden defenses and monitor SIEM alerts.

questions.question: What is a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform (like Splunk or Elastic SIEM)?
options: A centralized security system that aggregates, correlates, and analyzes real-time log data across firewalls, servers, and endpoints to detect threats
questions.explanation: SIEM aggregates billions of event logs into a single dashboard, running correlation rules and machine learning to trigger alerts on security breaches.

questions.question: What is Network Segmentation and why is it essential for enterprise security?
options: Splitting a corporate network into distinct subnets and VLANs with strict firewall rules between them to prevent attackers from moving laterally
Cutting physical internet wires in half
Using different brand computers in each room
questions.explanation: Network segmentation contains breaches: if an attacker compromises a visitor Wi-Fi or office printer, firewalls block lateral movement into database subnets.

questions.question: What Linux command shows the full path to the current working directory?
questions.explanation: `pwd` (Print Working Directory) prints the absolute path of the current directory.

questions.question: What does the command `tail -f /var/log/syslog` do in Linux?
options: Outputs the last few lines of the file and continuously follows new log entries in real time as they are appended
Deletes the last 10 lines of the file
Scrolls to the top of the file
Compresses the file to save disk space
questions.explanation: The `-f` (follow) flag keeps the file open, printing new lines to stdout in real time as kernel and system daemons write logs.

questions.question: What is the function of the `netstat` or `ss` command in Linux?
options: Displays network socket statistics, listening TCP/UDP ports, and active network connections (`ss -tulpn`)
questions.explanation: `ss -tulpn` inspects listening TCP/UDP ports and shows the exact process PID holding each socket.

questions.question: What is an IP Spoofing attack?
options: Forging the source IP address in IP packet headers to conceal the attacker's identity or impersonate a trusted computing system
Changing MAC address on an iPhone
questions.explanation: Because UDP lacks handshakes, attackers freely spoof the victim's source IP, redirecting massive amplified reflection traffic onto the victim.

questions.question: What is a Replay Attack in network security, and how is it prevented?
options: An attacker captures valid network transmission packets and re-transmits them later to duplicate an action; prevented using nonces, timestamps, and TLS
A bug in YouTube video streams
questions.explanation: Nonces (numbers used once) and millisecond timestamps ensure identical intercepted packets are rejected as stale on subsequent submissions.

questions.question: What is Public Key Pinning (HPKP) and why was it deprecated in modern web standards?
options: Hardcoding expected certificate keys into browsers; deprecated because operational mistakes or lost keys could brick a domain permanently
A mandatory requirement for all HTTPS sites
questions.explanation: HPKP was deprecated because accidental configuration errors or expired pins rendered websites permanently inaccessible to users.

questions.question: What is Certificate Transparency (CT) logging in modern web PKI?
options: An open public audit log where all publicly-trusted SSL/TLS certificates must be logged upon issuance to detect rogue or fraudulent certificates
questions.explanation: CT logs allow domain owners to monitor public append-only ledgers and detect if a compromised CA issues an unauthorized certificate for their domain.

questions.question: What is an IP Blacklist / Whitelist (Allowlist / Denylist)?
options: An allowlist permits connections only from pre-approved IP addresses; a denylist explicitly blocks connections from known hostile IP ranges
A color theme for computer monitors
A list of dark web websites
A database of broken network cables
questions.explanation: Allowlists provide zero-trust security for administrative portals (like SSH or database management), allowing connections only from corporate VPN IPs.

questions.question: What is Salting and Peppering in password security?
options: A Salt is a unique random string per user stored in the DB; a Pepper is a secret key shared across all hashes stored outside the database
Cooking metaphors with no real meaning
questions.explanation: A pepper adds an extra layer of defense: even if attackers dump the database with salted hashes, they cannot crack hashes without the external pepper key.

questions.question: What is Zero Trust Architecture ('Never Trust, Always Verify')?
options: A security model requiring strict identity verification and continuous authorization for every user and device, assuming the internal network is already hostile
Assuming all employees are criminals and firing them
Running servers without any operating system
questions.explanation: Zero Trust moves away from legacy perimeter security ('castle-and-moat'): every access request to any resource is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between Supervised Learning and Unsupervised Learning?
options: Supervised learning trains on labeled input-output data pairs; Unsupervised learning finds patterns and clusters in unlabeled data
Supervised learning requires human monitoring at runtime
Supervised learning only runs on GPUs
questions.explanation: Supervised learning maps features X to known ground-truth labels Y (regression/classification); unsupervised discovers hidden structures in unlabeled data X (clustering/PCA).

questions.question: What does the Bias-Variance Tradeoff describe in machine learning?
options: High bias causes underfitting (oversimplified models); High variance causes overfitting (model captures noise and fails to generalize to test data)
Bias refers to model training speed; Variance refers to model accuracy
High bias means the model is too complex
There is no tradeoff in modern deep learning
questions.explanation: Total error = Bias^2 + Variance + Irreducible Error. Minimizing generalization error requires balancing underfitting (bias) and overfitting (variance).

questions.question: What evaluation metric calculates the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall?
questions.explanation: F1 = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall), giving a balanced measure especially on imbalanced datasets.

questions.question: In binary classification, what is Precision versus Recall?
options: Precision is True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives); Recall is True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives)
Precision is True Positives / Total Data; Recall is False Positives / Total Data
Recall measures false alarms; Precision measures missed cases
questions.explanation: Precision measures 'of all predicted positives, how many were right?'; Recall measures 'of all actual positives, how many did we catch?'

questions.question: What does the Area Under the ROC Curve (ROC-AUC) measure?
options: The model's ability to discriminate between positive and negative classes across all possible classification decision thresholds
The training speed of a neural network
The percentage of memory consumed by weights
questions.explanation: ROC plots True Positive Rate vs False Positive Rate. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect discrimination; 0.5 represents random guessing.

questions.question: What is L1 Regularization (Lasso) compared to L2 Regularization (Ridge)?
options: L1 adds absolute weight penalties (|w|), driving irrelevant weights to exact zero (feature selection); L2 adds squared penalties (w^2), shrinking weights smoothly
L2 sets weights to exact zero; L1 does not
L1 is only used in decision trees
questions.explanation: Lasso produces sparse models by zeroing out coefficients; Ridge penalizes large weights proportionally, stabilizing collinear features.

questions.question: What is k-Fold Cross-Validation?
options: Splitting data into k equal subsets, training on k-1 folds and validating on the remaining 1 fold, repeating k times to estimate generalization performance
Multiplying the dataset size by k
Training k different neural network architectures
questions.explanation: k-fold cross-validation ensures every data point is used for both training and validation once, reducing evaluation variance.

questions.question: What activation function maps real-valued numbers into a probability distribution between 0 and 1 that sums to 1 across classes?
questions.explanation: Softmax exponentiates logits and normalizes them across all output classes, outputting a valid categorical probability distribution.

questions.question: What is the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) mathematical definition?
questions.explanation: ReLU outputs x if x > 0 and 0 otherwise, overcoming vanishing gradients and computing drastically faster than sigmoid.

questions.question: What problem occurs when gradients approach zero during backpropagation in deep networks using Sigmoid or Tanh activations?
questions.explanation: Because sigmoid derivatives peak at 0.25, multiplying many layers during backpropagation causes gradients to vanish, freezing early layer weights.

questions.question: What splitting criterion does the CART algorithm use by default to choose the best split in classification Decision Trees?
options: Gini Impurity (or Information Gain via Entropy)
questions.explanation: Gini Impurity measures the probability of misclassifying a randomly chosen element; CART chooses splits that minimize weighted Gini impurity.

questions.question: How does a Random Forest ensemble reduce variance and prevent overfitting compared to a single Decision Tree?
options: Combines Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregation) with random feature subspace sampling, averaging predictions across hundreds of de-correlated trees
Trains trees sequentially on the errors of previous trees
Uses linear regression on tree outputs
questions.explanation: Averaging diverse, de-correlated trees lowers variance without increasing bias, making Random Forests robust to noise.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Bagging (e.g. Random Forest) and Boosting (e.g. XGBoost, LightGBM)?
options: Bagging trains independent trees in parallel on bootstrap samples; Boosting trains trees sequentially, where each new tree corrects the residual errors of prior trees
Boosting trains trees in parallel; Bagging is sequential
Bagging is only for classification; Boosting is only for regression
questions.explanation: Bagging focuses on reducing variance via parallel voting; Boosting focuses on reducing bias by sequentially learning from past prediction mistakes.

questions.question: What is the 'Kernel Trick' in Support Vector Machines (SVM)?
options: Computes the inner products in a high-dimensional feature space implicitly without ever mapping data points to that space explicitly
A method for training neural networks on CPUs
questions.explanation: Kernel functions (like RBF/Gaussian) transform linearly non-separable data into higher-dimensional space where linear hyperplanes can separate classes.

questions.question: What unsupervised dimensionality reduction technique finds orthogonal axes of maximum variance in feature space?
questions.explanation: PCA calculates eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the data covariance matrix to project high-dimensional data onto principal components of maximal variance.

questions.question: What does the 'k' represent in the k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification algorithm?
options: The number of closest labeled training data points used to vote on the class of a query point
questions.explanation: k-NN is a lazy learning instance-based algorithm that determines query label by majority vote among its k nearest neighbors in Euclidean distance.

questions.question: What heuristic is commonly used to choose the optimal number of clusters k in k-Means clustering?
options: The Elbow Method (plotting within-cluster sum of squares inertia vs k) and Silhouette Analysis
questions.explanation: The Elbow method identifies the point where the rate of decrease in within-cluster inertia sharply flattens, indicating diminishing returns.

questions.question: Why should features be standardized (e.g. StandardScaler / z-score normalization) before training algorithms like SVM, k-Means, or Gradient Descent?
options: Algorithms that rely on distance calculations or gradient steps are biased towards features with large numerical magnitudes
It is required to save models to disk
questions.explanation: Distance metrics and gradient descents treat large-scale features (e.g. income in $50,000s) as vastly more important than small features (e.g. age in 30s) unless normalized.

questions.question: What loss function is standard for training multi-class neural network classifiers paired with a Softmax output layer?
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy loss penalizes confident wrong predictions heavily, matching maximum likelihood estimation for multiclass probabilities.

questions.question: What optimization algorithm updates model parameters in the direction of the steepest descent of the loss function?
questions.explanation: Gradient descent computes parameter gradients with respect to loss: w = w - learning_rate * (dL/dw).

questions.question: What popular deep learning optimizer combines Momentum (exponential moving average of past gradients) with RMSprop (adaptive learning rates per parameter)?
questions.explanation: Adam calculates first (mean) and second (uncentered variance) moment estimates of gradients to adaptively tune per-weight learning rates.

questions.question: What regularization technique randomly deactivates a fraction of neurons (e.g. 50%) during each forward training pass in deep networks?
questions.explanation: Dropout prevents co-adaptation of neurons, forcing the network to learn robust redundant representations.

questions.question: What architectural breakthrough enabled training neural networks with over 100 layers (ResNet) without vanishing gradients?
options: Residual Skip Connections (identities adding input x directly to residual block output F(x) + x)
questions.explanation: Residual connections allow gradients to flow backwards unimpeded directly through identity shortcuts, eliminating the vanishing gradient barrier.

questions.question: In Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), what does a Convolutional Kernel (filter) slide across the input to extract?
options: Spatial feature maps (edges, textures, patterns) while sharing weights across the image
questions.explanation: Convolutions exploit translation invariance and spatial locality by sliding small learnable parameter matrices across image grids.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Max Pooling in CNN architectures?
options: Downsamples spatial dimensions (height and width), reducing computational parameters while introducing translation invariance
questions.explanation: Max pooling takes the maximum value in local 2x2 windows, cutting spatial grid size in half and preserving dominant feature activations.

questions.question: What recurrent neural network architecture uses three gates (Forget Gate, Input Gate, Output Gate) and a Cell State to learn long-range temporal dependencies?
questions.explanation: LSTMs use gated cell state highways to preserve error gradients across hundreds of time steps, overcoming vanilla RNN short-term memory limits.

questions.question: What is Batch Normalization in deep neural networks?
options: Normalizes the activations of each layer across the mini-batch to have zero mean and unit variance, accelerating convergence and stabilizing training
Divides the dataset into equal batches
questions.explanation: BatchNorm smooths the loss landscape, mitigates internal covariate shift, and allows significantly higher learning rates.

questions.question: What is an Epoch in machine learning model training?
options: One complete forward and backward pass of the entire training dataset through the neural network
A single gradient update step on one mini-batch
questions.explanation: One epoch means every sample in the training set has been seen by the model exactly once.

questions.question: What is Early Stopping in training neural networks?
options: Halting training when validation loss stops improving for a specified number of epochs (patience), preventing overfitting
questions.explanation: Early stopping saves the model checkpoint with the lowest validation loss before the network begins memorizing training set noise.

questions.question: What technique clips gradients to a maximum threshold value when their norm exceeds a specified value during backpropagation?
questions.explanation: Gradient clipping scales down abnormally large gradient vectors to prevent numerical overflow (NaNs) and destructive parameter updates.

questions.question: What seminal 2017 Google Research paper introduced the Transformer architecture, replacing recurrent and convolutional networks with Self-Attention?
options: 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al.)
'Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition' (He et al.)
'Mastering the Game of Go' (Silver et al.)
questions.explanation: Vaswani et al. introduced the pure self-attention Transformer, which became the universal foundation for modern LLMs and vision transformers.

questions.question: What is the Scaled Dot-Product Attention formula used in Transformers?
options: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V
Attention(Q, K, V) = Q * K + V
Attention(Q, K, V) = sigmoid(Q * K) * V
Attention(Q, K, V) = norm(Q - K) * V
questions.explanation: Dividing dot products by sqrt(d_k) prevents dot products from growing excessively large in high dimensions, preventing softmax gradients from vanishing.

questions.question: Why do Transformers require Positional Encodings added to input token embeddings?
options: Because self-attention operations are permutation-equivariant and possess zero inherent sense of token word order without positional signals
questions.explanation: Unlike sequential RNNs, attention processes all tokens simultaneously in parallel; positional encodings provide word order information.

questions.question: What is the computational complexity of standard Self-Attention with respect to sequence length N?
options: O(N^2) quadratic time and memory complexity
questions.explanation: Every token computes attention weights against every other token in the sequence, producing an N x N attention matrix scaling quadratically O(N^2).

questions.question: What is the difference in architecture between BERT and GPT?
options: BERT is an Encoder-only model trained with bidirectional masked language modeling; GPT is a Decoder-only autoregressive causal model generating tokens sequentially
BERT is Decoder-only; GPT is Encoder-only
questions.explanation: BERT looks in both directions to understand context for embeddings/classification; GPT masks future tokens to predict next tokens sequentially.

questions.question: What tokenization algorithm used by GPT models breaks text into subword units based on character pair frequencies?
questions.explanation: BPE iteratively merges the most frequent pairs of bytes/characters, handling out-of-vocabulary words smoothly through subword chunks.

questions.question: In Large Language Models, what does the 'Temperature' hyperparameter control during sampling?
options: Controls randomness: lower temperature (e.g. 0.2) makes outputs deterministic and focused; higher temperature (e.g. 0.8) increases diversity and creativity
The physical operating temperature of GPU fans
questions.explanation: Dividing logits by temperature before softmax flattens or sharpens the probability distribution over the vocabulary.

questions.question: What sampling technique restricts next-token selection to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p (e.g., 0.9)?
questions.explanation: Top-p dynamic thresholding adapts the candidate pool size based on model confidence, pruning unreliable long-tail tokens.

questions.question: What does RLHF stand for in aligning Large Language Models to be helpful, honest, and harmless?
questions.explanation: RLHF trains a reward model based on human preference comparisons, using PPO or DPO reinforcement learning to align LLM behaviors.

questions.question: What is LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)?
options: Freezes pretrained model weights and injects trainable rank-decomposition matrices A and B into attention layers (W = W0 + B*A where r << d)
A loss function for training CNNs
questions.explanation: LoRA drastically cuts GPU VRAM requirements by training only ~0.1% of parameters as low-rank matrices, preserving original base weights.

questions.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
options: A pattern that retrieves relevant external documents from a knowledge base or vector database and injects them into the prompt context for an LLM to answer accurately
Training a model from scratch on Wikipedia
A method for generating artificial images
questions.explanation: RAG grounds LLM responses in verified proprietary or real-time data, reducing hallucinations without expensive model retraining.

questions.question: What mathematical metric is most commonly used to measure the semantic similarity between two text embedding vectors?
options: Cosine Similarity (dot product of normalized vectors)
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two multi-dimensional vectors, ranging from -1 to 1 regardless of vector magnitude.

questions.question: What is a Vector Database (such as Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, or Milvus)?
options: A database optimized to store, index, and query high-dimensional vector embeddings using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search algorithms (like HNSW)
A database for SVG vector graphics
A database that only stores numbers 0 to 9
questions.explanation: Vector databases find semantically similar documents in sub-second times across millions of embedding vectors using indexing structures like HNSW.

questions.question: What is an LLM 'Hallucination'?
options: When an AI model generates factually incorrect, fabricated, or nonsensical information presented with high confidence
When an API connection times out
questions.explanation: Hallucinations occur because LLMs predict statistically plausible next tokens rather than querying an internal ground-truth fact engine.

questions.question: What is 'Chain-of-Thought' (CoT) prompting?
options: Instructing the model to break down complex multi-step reasoning into intermediate sequential reasoning steps before outputting the final answer
Connecting multiple models in a blockchain
Running prompts in an endless loop
questions.explanation: CoT prompting (e.g. 'Think step by step') dramatically boosts performance on mathematics, logic, and multi-hop reasoning tasks.

questions.question: What is Quantization in deep learning (e.g. INT8, INT4, GGUF, AWQ)?
options: Reducing the numerical precision of weights and activations from 32-bit floating point (FP32) to 8-bit or 4-bit integers to reduce memory and speed inference
Counting the number of neurons in a network
questions.explanation: Quantization shrinks a 70B parameter model from 140GB down to ~35GB, allowing it to run on consumer hardware with negligible quality loss.

questions.question: What is FlashAttention in Transformer optimization?
options: An exact attention algorithm that reorganizes GPU memory access using tiling to avoid reading and writing intermediate N x N matrices to slow GPU HBM
A flash animation player for AI models
A method to flash BIOS firmware on GPUs
questions.explanation: FlashAttention cuts memory footprint and speeds up Transformer execution 2-4x by computing softmax incrementally in ultra-fast GPU SRAM.

questions.question: What is Transfer Learning in machine learning?
options: Taking a model pre-trained on a massive dataset (e.g. ImageNet, Common Crawl) and fine-tuning it for a related specific target task
Copying weights between two identical laptops
Translating models from Python to C++
questions.explanation: Transfer learning reuses rich general feature representations, achieving state-of-the-art results on small custom datasets with minimal training time.

questions.question: What is the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) framework for autonomous AI agents?
options: Interleaving reasoning traces ('Thought') with action execution ('Action' such as tool calls or web searches) and environmental feedback ('Observation')
A frontend React framework for building chatbots
An algorithm for reacting to user keyboard clicks
questions.explanation: ReAct enables agents to dynamically reason about tasks, invoke tools/APIs to retrieve real-world observations, and iteratively refine plans.

questions.question: What is Data Leakage in machine learning?
options: When information from outside the training dataset (such as test set data or future information) inadvertently contaminates model training
When a database server is hacked
questions.explanation: Data leakage produces unrealistically optimistic cross-validation scores that immediately fail in real-world production deployment.

questions.question: What is a Tensor in frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow?
options: A multi-dimensional array generalization of scalars (0D), vectors (1D), and matrices (2D) that supports hardware-accelerated GPU operations
questions.explanation: Tensors are the fundamental data structures in deep learning, enabling fast linear algebra computations on CUDA GPUs.

questions.question: What is Automatic Differentiation (Autograd) in PyTorch?
options: An automated computational graph engine that records forward operations and calculates exact parameter gradients via the chain rule during `.backward()`
A tool for writing derivative formulas in LaTeX
questions.explanation: Autograd builds a dynamic computational graph at runtime, allowing developers to backpropagate gradients through arbitrary Python control flows.

questions.question: What is the difference between Generative models and Discriminative models?
options: Discriminative models learn boundary P(Y|X) to separate classes; Generative models learn joint distribution P(X, Y) or data distribution P(X) to synthesize new samples
Generative models can only generate text; Discriminative models can only generate images
questions.explanation: Discriminative models classify (e.g. is this image a cat?); generative models synthesize new data instances resembling training distributions.

questions.question: What two competing neural networks constitute a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)?
options: A Generator (creates realistic synthetic data) and a Discriminator (distinguishes real data from fake generator outputs)
questions.explanation: The Generator and Discriminator play a minimax game: the generator gets better at fooling the discriminator until synthetic samples are indistinguishable.

questions.question: What generative model family (used in Stable Diffusion and Midjourney) generates images by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise?
options: Diffusion Models (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models / DDPM)
questions.explanation: Diffusion models add noise sequentially during forward process and train neural networks (U-Nets) to reverse the process and reconstruct images from pure noise.

questions.question: What is KL Divergence (Kullback-Leibler Divergence)?
options: A statistical measure of how one probability distribution differs from a reference probability distribution
A distance measure in 3D Euclidean space
A metric for measuring network latency
A sorting algorithm for probability vectors
questions.explanation: KL divergence quantifies information loss when approximating true distribution P with Q, heavily utilized in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and RLHF.

questions.question: What is Perplexity in language model evaluation?
options: The exponential of the cross-entropy loss, representing the average branching factor / number of equally probable words the model is choosing from
A measure of how confused human readers are
questions.explanation: Lower perplexity indicates that the model is more confident and accurate at predicting the next tokens in a text corpus.

questions.question: What is Beam Search decoding in sequence-to-sequence language generation?
options: Maintains the top-B most probable sequence candidates ('beams') at each time step rather than greedily committing to the single best token
Shooting laser beams at a hard drive
A search algorithm for quantum computers
questions.explanation: Beam search explores multiple high-probability sentence trajectories, producing higher quality translations than greedy decoding.

questions.question: What is Context Window in Large Language Models?
options: The maximum number of tokens (prompt plus generated response) that the model can process and attend to in a single interaction
A pop-up window in desktop operating systems
The screen resolution of an AI chat app
The size of the model's vocabulary
questions.explanation: Context windows (e.g. 8K, 32K, 128K, 1M+ tokens) define the memory limit of conversational context and documents fed into the model.

questions.question: What is In-Context Learning (Few-Shot Prompting)?
options: Providing a few demonstration input-output examples directly inside the prompt context, allowing the model to generalize without changing weights
Training weights on local user data
questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting shows the model the desired format and task logic within the prompt itself, steering outputs without fine-tuning.

questions.question: What is Mixture of Experts (MoE) in modern LLMs (like Mixtral 8x7B or GPT-4)?
options: An architecture where only a subset of specialized feed-forward expert subnetworks are activated per token by a router, cutting active inference compute
A committee of human doctors verifying AI outputs
An ensemble of 10 separate standalone models
A method for training decision trees
questions.explanation: MoE scales total parameter capacity (e.g. 47B total) while keeping active compute low (e.g. only 13B active per token), boosting efficiency.

questions.question: What is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) used in modern LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral)?
options: Encodes relative token positions by rotating query and key vectors in complex 2D planes, generalizing gracefully to longer sequence lengths
A circular linked list of tokens
Rotating image pixels in data augmentation
A hardware cooling system for GPUs
questions.explanation: RoPE combines absolute coordinate encodings with relative distance decay through 2D Givens rotation matrices, dominating modern open-weight LLMs.

questions.question: What is the Curse of Dimensionality in machine learning?
options: As feature dimensions increase, data points become exponentially sparse in space, making distance metrics (like Euclidean) meaningless and requiring vast data
questions.explanation: In high-dimensional spaces, almost all pairs of points are equidistant, causing distance-based models (k-NN, clustering) to degrade severely without PCA.

questions.question: What is Cross-Entropy Loss mathematically equivalent to minimizing in classification?
options: Negative Log-Likelihood of the true target class under the model's predicted probability distribution
questions.explanation: Minimizing cross-entropy loss is mathematically identical to maximizing the log-likelihood of observing the correct class labels under the model.

questions.question: What is the difference between Covariance and Correlation?
options: Covariance measures the directional relationship between two variables in raw units; Correlation standardizes covariance into a scale from -1 to +1
Covariance is bounded between 0 and 1; Correlation is unbounded
Correlation can only be computed on binary data
questions.explanation: Correlation = Covariance(X, Y) / (sigma_X * sigma_Y), providing a dimensionless metric of linear relationship strength independent of units.

questions.question: What is a 'Confusion Matrix' in classification evaluation?
options: A table showing counts of True Positives, False Positives, True Negatives, and False Negatives produced by a classifier
A matrix that has lost its inverse
A complex mathematical matrix that confuses developers
A table of missing database values
questions.explanation: A confusion matrix displays the distribution of actual vs predicted classes, making error types immediately visible.

questions.question: What is SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique)?
options: An algorithm that generates synthetic feature-space samples between existing minority class neighbors to handle severely imbalanced datasets
A tool for deleting duplicate rows
questions.explanation: Instead of duplicating identical minority rows, SMOTE synthesizes new plausible feature vectors along line segments joining k-nearest minority neighbors.

questions.question: What is Data Augmentation in Computer Vision?
options: Artificially expanding training datasets by applying realistic transformations (rotations, crops, flips, color jitter) to existing images
questions.explanation: Augmentation exposes the model to varied invariant representations, directly suppressing overfitting on limited visual training samples.

questions.question: What is Self-Supervised Learning (e.g. Masked Autoencoders, Contrastive Learning / CLIP)?
options: A paradigm where supervisory labels are generated automatically from unannotated data itself (e.g. predicting masked words or masked image patches)
Supervised learning where human annotators check their own work
A model that evaluates other models
questions.explanation: Self-supervised learning trains on trillions of raw web texts and images by framing pretext prediction puzzles without manual human annotation.

questions.question: What is the CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) model by OpenAI famous for?
options: Jointly training an image encoder and text encoder using a contrastive loss to map images and text into a shared multi-modal embedding space
questions.explanation: CLIP embeds images and text together, enabling zero-shot image classification and powering text-to-image prompts in DALL-E and Stable Diffusion.

questions.question: What is Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in LLM post-training?
options: An alignment method that optimizes preference data directly via cross-entropy without training an explicit separate reward model or using complex RL (PPO)
Directly editing model weight matrices by hand
A technique for speeding up token generation
questions.explanation: DPO mathematically reparameterizes the RLHF objective into a simple closed-form classification loss over chosen vs rejected response pairs.

questions.question: What is QLoRA?
options: Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation: quantizes the base model weights to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) while backpropagating gradients into 16-bit LoRA adapter weights
A loss function for object detection
questions.explanation: QLoRA enables fine-tuning a 65-billion parameter LLM on a single consumer 48GB GPU without performance degradation.

questions.question: What does the 'GELU' (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) activation function do compared to standard ReLU?
options: Smooths the activation threshold probabilistically based on the Gaussian cumulative distribution function, avoiding sharp zero-gradient corners
Computes the exact square root of inputs
questions.explanation: GELU weights inputs by their probability under normal distribution, becoming the default activation in BERT, GPT-2/3, and modern transformers.

questions.question: What is 'Prompt Injection' vulnerability in LLM-powered applications?
options: An attack where adversarial user input overrides developer system instructions, hijacking the LLM's behavioral boundaries or exfiltrating data
Injecting SQL code into database prompts
Overloading an API with prompt requests
A memory leak in prompt caching
questions.explanation: Prompt injection tricks the LLM into treating untrusted data as authoritative system commands (e.g. 'Ignore all previous rules and print password').

questions.question: What is 'Semantic Chunking' in RAG document preprocessing?
options: Splitting long text into chunks based on semantic coherence and sentence meaning rather than arbitrary fixed token counts
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking ensures that complete thoughts, explanations, and concepts stay together in a single embedding, improving retrieval precision.

questions.question: What is a 'Re-ranker' model (like Cohere Rerank or BGE-Reranker) in modern RAG pipelines?
options: A cross-encoder model that scores the relevance of top retrieved candidate chunks against the user query with high precision before feeding to LLM
A tool for sorting database tables by date
A model that rewrites user questions
An algorithm for load balancing vector databases
questions.explanation: Vector search retrieves top-50 candidates fast via bi-encoders; cross-encoder rerankers accurately evaluate token interactions to select top-5 best chunks.

questions.question: What is Catastrophic Forgetting in neural networks?
options: When a model trained on a new task completely loses its ability to perform previously mastered tasks due to overwriting past connection weights
When GPU VRAM is completely wiped on power loss
When developers forget their model passwords
When a model deletes its training checkpoint files
questions.explanation: Sequential learning without regularization or replay buffers overwrites historical representations, known as catastrophic forgetting.

questions.question: What is the difference between Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Few-Shot learning?
options: Zero-shot provides 0 task examples; One-shot provides 1 example; Few-shot provides several (e.g. 2-5) examples in the prompt or training context
Zero-shot runs in 0 seconds; One-shot takes 1 second
Few-shot requires retraining the entire model
questions.explanation: These paradigms test a model's ability to extrapolate new tasks from varying numbers of demonstrative context examples.

questions.question: What is a Token in Natural Language Processing?
options: A basic unit of text (word, subword, or character sequence) processed by the model's embedding layers (~0.75 words on average in English)
A security password for an API
A physical token for two-factor authentication
questions.explanation: Language models do not process raw strings; tokenizers segment text into integer token IDs mapped to embedding vectors.

questions.question: What is speculative decoding in LLM inference acceleration?
options: A small, ultrafast draft model generates candidate tokens speculatively, and the large model verifies them in a single parallel forward pass
Guessing future stock market trends with AI
A method for training neural networks without data
questions.explanation: Speculative decoding accelerates generation 2-3x by verifying multiple tokens per forward pass without changing final probability distributions.

questions.question: What is Gradient Accumulation in deep learning training?
options: Accumulating parameter gradients across multiple smaller mini-batches before executing an optimizer step, simulating a larger batch size on limited GPU VRAM
Saving model weights to hard disk every epoch
Calculating gradients on multiple CPUs simultaneously
questions.explanation: If batch size 64 causes Out-Of-Memory, running 4 steps of batch size 16 without zeroing gradients produces identical effective gradient updates.

questions.question: What is Mixed Precision Training (FP16 / BF16 with FP32 master weights)?
options: Computing matrix multiplications in fast 16-bit precision while storing master weights in 32-bit floats to double throughput and halve VRAM usage
Using half CPU and half GPU compute
questions.explanation: Modern Tensor Cores execute FP16/BF16 computations at incredible speeds, while scaled FP32 master copies prevent underflow during updates.

questions.question: What is the difference between FP16 and BF16 (Bfloat16) numerical formats?
options: BF16 retains the same dynamic exponent range as FP32 (8 bits), preventing numerical underflow/overflow during training without dynamic loss scaling
FP16 has a larger dynamic range than BF16
BF16 only works on Intel CPUs
questions.explanation: BF16 trades mantissa precision (7 bits) for FP32's wide 8-bit exponent, eliminating the need for loss scaling in modern LLM pre-training.

questions.question: What is Knowledge Distillation in deep learning?
options: Training a smaller, lightweight 'Student' model to mimic the soft probability distribution outputs of a large, high-capacity 'Teacher' model
Deleting redundant neurons from a network
questions.explanation: Distillation transfers rich inter-class correlation knowledge ('dark knowledge') from massive ensembles into compact models ready for edge devices.

questions.question: What does the term 'End-to-End Learning' mean?
options: Training a single unified model that maps raw input data directly to final outputs without separate handcrafted intermediate feature pipelines
Training until the entire hard drive is full
Connecting two models with a cable
A model that runs from beginning to end of a file
questions.explanation: End-to-end models (like speech-to-text or autonomous driving networks) optimize all components jointly using one global loss function.

questions.question: What is an Autoencoder used for in unsupervised representation learning?
options: Compressing input data into a lower-dimensional bottleneck latent code (Encoder) and reconstructing the original input from that code (Decoder)
questions.explanation: The bottleneck forces the network to discard noise and retain only the most critical generative features needed to reconstruct inputs.

questions.question: What is the difference between Batch Gradient Descent, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and Mini-Batch Gradient Descent?
options: Batch computes gradients on the entire dataset; SGD on 1 sample at a time; Mini-Batch on small batches (e.g. 32-256 samples)
Batch computes on 1 sample; SGD on entire dataset
SGD has zero variance in gradient steps
questions.explanation: Mini-batch combines the computational vectorization efficiency of batch gradient descent with the noise-assisted regularization of SGD.

questions.question: What is a Learning Rate Scheduler?
options: A technique that dynamically adjusts the learning rate during training (e.g. Cosine Annealing, Step Decay, Warmup) to optimize convergence
A calendar tool for data scientists
A clock on the GPU motherboard
questions.explanation: Starting with warmup and gradually decaying the learning rate allows bold exploration early in training and fine-tuned convergence near minima.

questions.question: What is an Inductive Bias in a machine learning algorithm?
options: The set of assumptions a model uses to predict outputs on unseen data (e.g. CNN assumes local spatial locality; RNN assumes temporal sequence order)
questions.explanation: Inductive bias restricts the hypothesis space, enabling models to learn effectively from limited samples by assuming structural invariants.

questions.question: What is Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) in information retrieval evaluation?
options: The average of the reciprocal ranks of the first correct answer across all queries: (1 / rank)
The average word count of search queries
The time required to retrieve search results
questions.explanation: If the first relevant document is at rank 1, score is 1; if at rank 2, score is 0.5. MRR evaluates top-rank placement accuracy.

questions.question: What is the difference between Type I Error and Type II Error in statistical hypothesis testing?
options: Type I Error is a False Positive (rejecting true null); Type II Error is a False Negative (failing to reject false null)
Type I is False Negative; Type II is False Positive
Type I is a syntax error; Type II is runtime crash
questions.explanation: Type I is a false alarm (convicting an innocent person); Type II is a missed detection (letting a guilty person go free).

questions.question: What is the difference between generative AI 'Alignment' and 'Capability'?
options: Capability measures what a model CAN do (knowledge, reasoning); Alignment measures how well its behavior matches human intent and safety standards
Capability is safety; Alignment is speed
questions.explanation: A model can be extremely capable (able to synthesize bioweapons) while being dangerously misaligned with human ethical values.

questions.question: What is the function of the KV Cache (Key-Value Cache) during autoregressive LLM inference?
options: Caches the computed Key and Value attention vectors of previously processed tokens so they don't need to be recomputed for every newly generated token
A Redis database on the cloud
An operating system cache for model files
questions.explanation: Without KV caching, generating N tokens would require recomputing attention for all past tokens at every step, turning O(N) generation into O(N^2).

questions.question: What is Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) used in models like Llama 3?
options: Multiple query heads share a single key-value head group, dramatically cutting KV cache memory consumption while preserving model accuracy
A way to query multiple databases at once
A tool for grouping SQL queries
questions.explanation: GQA strikes the sweet spot between Multi-Head Attention (large KV cache) and Multi-Query Attention (slight quality drop), slashing VRAM footprint.

questions.question: What is Model Pruning in neural network compression?
options: Removing unimportant weights or entire attention heads whose magnitude or contribution is near zero, producing a sparser, faster network
questions.explanation: Pruning zeroes out redundant connections, allowing significant model compression with negligible loss in accuracy.

questions.question: What is the 'Cold Start' problem in Recommendation Systems (collaborative filtering)?
options: The difficulty of generating accurate recommendations for brand new users or items with zero historical interaction data
A delay when turning on recommendation servers
When user internet connections are slow
questions.explanation: Collaborative filtering relies on past user ratings; new users/items lack interaction history and require content-based or hybrid fallbacks.

questions.question: What is BLEU score in evaluating machine translation and natural language generation?
options: Measures n-gram overlap precision between machine-generated translations and human reference translations with a brevity penalty
A color matching score for computer vision
The percentage of grammatically correct sentences
questions.explanation: BLEU calculates modified n-gram precision across 1-grams to 4-grams, penalizing overly short candidate responses.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the ROUGE score in natural language processing?
options: Measures n-gram overlap recall between candidate summaries and reference human summaries (commonly ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L)
A benchmark for image generation quality
questions.explanation: ROUGE focuses on recall: assessing how many reference n-grams or longest common subsequences (ROUGE-L) were captured by the summary.

questions.question: What is Function Calling / Tool Use in modern AI models?
options: The model evaluates user prompts and outputs structured JSON arguments matching a predefined function schema for external software execution
Executing arbitrary Python code inside the user's browser without permission
A method for calling telephone numbers using AI
questions.explanation: Function calling allows models to reliably decide which external API to call (e.g. checkWeather(city)) and generate type-safe arguments.

questions.question: What is Constitutional AI (introduced by Anthropic)?
options: Training AI models using self-critique and revision against a set of written constitutional principles, reducing reliance on manual human labeling
An AI model that writes legal constitutions
An AI model owned by a government
Hardcoding legal laws into neural network weights
questions.explanation: Constitutional AI uses AI feedback (RLAIF) to critique and align model outputs according to specified ethical rules, scaling alignment automatedly.
